questions.question: Many Spaniards study a set syllabus for years and sit exams against thousands of rivals to win a permanent post. What are they doing?
hints: The prize is a job working for the state.
People talk about “sacarse la plaza” (landing the post).
It comes from “oposiciones”.
questions.fun_fact: There are oposiciones for almost everything: teachers, firefighters, judges, police officers and even jobs at Correos, the Spanish post office.

media.credit: Gary Todd · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gary Todd

questions.description: A cane that isn't for walking, yet the whole town respects it.
questions.question: At the swearing-in at a Spanish town hall, the vara de mando (a ceremonial staff) is handed over. What does it stand for?
wrong_answers: The authority of the justice of the peace
The authority of the town clerk
The authority of the festivities councilor
hints: It is handed over at the council meeting, right after a vote.
The staff usually bears the town's coat of arms and some tassels.
It is carried by whoever holds the most important seat on the town council.
questions.fun_fact: Many mayors only bring out the vara de mando for solemn occasions, such as the processions of the town's patron saint festivities.

media.credit: Ivanhercaz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ivanhercaz

questions.description: Some jobs get passed down like grandma's sofa, but this one comes with a throne.
questions.question: Every year at the Princess of Asturias Awards ceremony in Oviedo, the heir to the throne gives a speech. Who is she?
hints: She was born in Madrid in 2005.
She studied in Wales and then at military academies.
She is the older sister of Infanta Sofía.
questions.fun_fact: Leonor swore to uphold the Constitution before the Spanish parliament on October 31, 2023, her 18th birthday.

media.credit: vicenmiranda from Oviedo, España · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: vicenmiranda from Oviedo, España

questions.description: The birthday when the cake comes with paperwork.
questions.question: The Spanish Constitution sets me at 18. What am I?
wrong_answers: The age you finish the ESO
The age a DNI becomes required
hints: I appear in Article 12 of the Constitution.
From that day on, you can vote in elections.
I make you an adult in the eyes of the law.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1978, you didn't come of age in Spain until you turned 21.

media.credit: Almanaque Lusofonista · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Almanaque Lusofonista

questions.description: A golden detail that has gone on and off the coat of arms, depending on who was in charge.
questions.question: It's golden, it sits at the top of Spain's coat of arms, and the Second Republic swapped it for a city wall. What is it?
hints: It has to do with who the head of state is.
It stands for the monarchy.
The king in the Spanish deck of cards wears it on his head.
questions.fun_fact: On top of the crown on the coat of arms sits a small globe with a cross, a symbol of the king's power.

media.credit: Selbymay · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Selbymay

questions.description: A singer, an anthem with no words and a pen: what could go wrong?
questions.question: Marta Sánchez sang her own lyrics to Spain's national anthem at a concert in Madrid. In what year?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
The video spread like wildfire on WhatsApp and Instagram.
It was the year Pedro Sánchez became Prime Minister of Spain.
questions.fun_fact: In 2008 the Spanish Olympic Committee tried to give the anthem official lyrics, but withdrew them a few days later.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: A coat of arms with more tenants than a Madrid apartment block.
questions.question: This is Spain's coat of arms. Which old kingdom does the golden castle on a red background stand for?
hints: Its historic capital was Burgos.
Isabella I, the Catholic Queen, was its queen.
Its name sounds almost the same as the picture.
questions.fun_fact: At the bottom of the coat of arms there is a pomegranate (granada in Spanish), standing for the Kingdom of Granada, conquered in 1492.

media.credit: Gobierno de España · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gobierno de España

questions.description: Carvings painted so well you feel like asking them if they're cold.
questions.question: On the carvings in Valladolid's National Museum of Sculpture, the skin was painted in oils with its natural color and shine. What is this technique called?
hints: It is a technique for painting wooden religious statues.
It is different from the one used to paint the robes with gold.
Its name comes from the Spanish word “carne,” meaning flesh.
questions.fun_fact: Some image-carvers gave their statues glass eyes, ivory teeth and even tears made of resin.

media.credit: GFreihalter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: GFreihalter

questions.description: A girl who brings the milk and, while she's at it, wraps up a sixty-year career.
questions.question: This painting, “The Milkmaid of Bordeaux”, was painted around 1827 by a Spanish painter living in exile in that French city. Who?
hints: He was from Aragon.
He died in Bordeaux in 1828, aged over 80.
Earlier he had painted the Black Paintings at the Quinta del Sordo.
questions.fun_fact: Goya died in Bordeaux in 1828, and his remains did not return to Spain until 1899.

media.credit: Francisco Goya · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Francisco Goya

questions.description: Everyone says they hate it, and everyone knows the chorus by heart.
questions.question: It plays nonstop at chiringuitos (beach bars) and parties, has an easy dance, and by September everyone forgets it. What is it called in Spain?
hints: It has to do with a season of the year.
Every year, journalists try to guess which one it will be.
It's the one for vacation, sunshine and the beach.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has been picking one of these songs every year for decades, since the days of Georgie Dann and “La barbacoa”.

media.credit: Tyk · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tyk

questions.description: A voice from the Costa del Sol with more tan than a lifeguard in August.
questions.question: I was the voice of Danza Invisible, the band from Torremolinos that hit it big with “Sabor de amor”. Who am I?
hints: I'm Andalusian, from the Costa del Sol.
My band was a hit in the 1980s with very danceable songs.
My surname starts with O.
questions.fun_fact: Danza Invisible started out in Torremolinos in the early 1980s with a darker sound, before switching to the Latin rhythms of “Sabor de amor”.

media.credit: Jl FilpoC · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jl FilpoC

questions.description: Two friends from Barcelona more popular than sandwiches on a school trip.
questions.question: Which Barcelona duo, with Quimi Portet as one half, sang “Insurrección” and split up in 1998?
hints: Before that, they had played together in the band Los Rápidos.
They also sang “Como un burro amarrado en la puerta del baile”.
The other member of the duo was Manolo García.
questions.fun_fact: They said goodbye in 1998, but in 2026 El Último de la Fila got back together for a tour with stadium concerts.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Twelve points to anyone who gets this one without cheating.
questions.question: Which singer represented Spain at Eurovision 1997 with the song “Sin rencor”?
hints: He's a Catalan singer.
He came sixth, one of Spain's best results in the 1990s.
His father is also a singer, famous for his boleros.
questions.fun_fact: Marcos Llunas is the son of Dyango, the bolero singer famous for “Corazón mágico”.

media.credit: Michael Doherty · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Doherty

questions.description: A city with so much rock that even the pigeons wear earplugs.
questions.question: In me, Eva and Juan teamed up in 1992 to form Amaral, and before them Héroes del Silencio came from my streets. What city am I?
hints: I'm in northern Spain, but not by the sea.
The Ebro River flows through me.
I'm the capital of Aragon.
questions.fun_fact: Amaral is named after its singer, Eva Amaral; the other half of the duo is guitarist Juan Aguirre.

media.credit: Tyler Savitski · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tyler Savitski

questions.description: A bandit who stole hearts instead of stagecoaches.
questions.question: Which singer, son of the bullfighter Luis Miguel Dominguín, was a hit in the 1980s with “Amante bandido”?
hints: His mother was an Italian actress.
He also sang “Bambú” and “Te amaré”.
His mother, Miss Italy 1947, starred in films by Antonioni.
questions.fun_fact: His godfather at his baptism was the Italian film director Luchino Visconti.

media.credit: pere prlpz · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: pere prlpz

questions.description: The friend who always ends up as the victim of the latest prank.
questions.question: This Spanish YouTuber got famous playing games and goofing around in the videos of his close friend El Rubius. Who is he?
hints: He has his own channel, but many people know him mostly from his friend's videos.
His nickname is a short form of his real name.
His real name is Miguel Ángel.
questions.fun_fact: Mangel has appeared in so many of El Rubius's videos that many fans see them as an inseparable duo.

media.credit: SeriphSeraph · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SeriphSeraph

questions.description: More people staring at one screen than live in many Spanish cities put together.
questions.question: TheGrefg unveiled his own Fortnite skin to almost 2.5 million people at once, a Twitch record at the time. In what year?
hints: It happened in January.
It was right in the middle of the pandemic.
It was just after the lockdown year.
questions.fun_fact: The next year, Ibai beat that number with “La Velada del Año”, a boxing event between streamers.

media.credit: Michael Dorausch from Venice · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Dorausch from Venice

questions.description: Back when radio was so new that people listened with headphones and a look of pure amazement.
questions.question: Radio Barcelona, call sign EAJ-1, was Spain's first licensed radio station. In what year did it start broadcasting?
hints: It was in the “Roaring Twenties”.
It was during the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera.
It was one year before the middle of that decade.
questions.fun_fact: Radio Barcelona is still on the air and today is part of Cadena SER.

media.credit: Archives of the Finnish Broadcasting Company Yle · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Archives of the Finnish Broadcasting Company Yle

questions.description: A word with more centuries behind it than the tortilla de patatas, and more trips than a suitcase at an airport.
questions.question: It's a Canary Islands word that recalls an ancient Germanic people and is said half-jokingly. Where is someone called a “godo” in the Canaries from?
hints: The Goths were a people who came to Hispania from northern Europe.
To a Canary Islander, this person comes from outside the islands.
They arrive by plane or boat from Madrid, Seville or Valladolid.
questions.fun_fact: The Visigoths ruled Hispania until the year 711, with their capital in Toledo.

media.credit: Ingo Mehling · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ingo Mehling

questions.description: Some holidays on the calendar are good for much more than a long weekend.
questions.question: You hear it all over Spain, and it's named after a holiday. What does “hacerle la pascua” to someone mean?
hints: It has nothing to do with bunnies or chocolate eggs.
It's an old expression that grandparents still use a lot.
It means the same as “chincharle” or “jorobarle”.
questions.fun_fact: There's also “y santas pascuas”, which means “and that's the end of it”.

media.credit: Rowanwindwhistler · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rowanwindwhistler

questions.description: A little tube that turns any milkshake into a lung workout.
questions.question: It's a thin little tube for sipping juice or a milkshake, and these days it's often made of paper. What is it called in Spain?
hints: It usually sits in the glass of a soft drink.
Other Spanish-speaking countries have very different names for it.
Long ago it was made from dry cereal stalks.
questions.fun_fact: Before plastic, these tubes were made from dry rye stalks, which is how both “pajita” (from “paja”) and the English “straw” got their names.

media.credit: David Adam Kess · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Adam Kess

questions.description: A compliment so teeny-tiny it fits in your jacket pocket.
questions.question: If someone calls you «guapín» quite naturally, where are they most likely from?
hints: Look at the diminutive ending.
People there say «pequeñín» and «poquitín» all the time.
It's the land of fabada and the Picos de Europa.
questions.fun_fact: The -ín diminutive is so Asturian that even names get shortened that way: «Xuanín», «Pepín».

media.credit: Nick Hillier nhillier · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nick Hillier nhillier

questions.description: A garden tenant who never pays the rent.
questions.question: It lives under damp stones, it's grayish, has fourteen tiny legs and a body made of plates. What is it called in many parts of Spain?
hints: It often turns up when you lift a flowerpot or a log.
If you touch it, it rolls itself up.
Its name says what it turns into when it gets scared.
questions.fun_fact: The bicho bola isn't an insect: it's a crustacean, like crabs, even though it lives on dry land.

media.credit: Daderot · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daderot

questions.description: An ending that isn't big, but has plenty of character.
questions.question: This diminutive ending is heard a lot in Aragon and Murcia, and also in Granada and Almería. Which one is it?
hints: You hear it in Aragonese jota songs.
In Zaragoza, people add it when they ask for «un poco».
«Momentico», «pequeñico», «majico».
questions.fun_fact: Costa Ricans are called «ticos» because they use this diminutive all the time: «chiquitico», «momentico».

media.credit: Willtron · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Willtron

questions.description: A diminutive with a poquete of sparkle and plenty of party spirit.
questions.question: In the Spanish of one Mediterranean region with three provinces and its own language, you often hear «poquete» and «chiquete». Which one?
hints: In the region's other language, the diminutive ends in «-et».
Its capital is the third-largest city in Spain.
Its capital is famous for paella.
questions.fun_fact: In Valencian, «xiquet» means “kid”, and Valencian human towers are called «muixeranga».

media.credit: Nattes à chat · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nattes à chat

questions.description: A question to keep your T-shirt from flying away.
questions.question: You're doing the laundry: a hanger is to the closet as a clothespin is to the…
hints: Think about where each object is used.
The clothespin holds wet clothes so they can dry.
It's stretched between two posts, and you hang wet laundry on it to dry outside.
questions.fun_fact: In Argentina a clothespin is called a «broche», and in Colombia a «gancho».

media.credit: Almanta · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Almanta

questions.description: Four stripes in perfect order, better behaved than a line of schoolkids.
questions.question: Its flag has four horizontal stripes, red, white, green and yellow, adopted with its 1982 Statute. Which region is it?
hints: It's a single-province region in northern Spain.
The Ebro River runs through it.
Its capital is Logroño.
questions.fun_fact: La Rioja is the smallest autonomous community on the Spanish mainland.

media.credit: Toufaut Yuem Shumda · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Toufaut Yuem Shumda

questions.description: A flag with more history than a whole textbook.
questions.question: The red and yellow stripes on the Balearic flag recall the Crown of Aragon. Which king conquered Majorca in 1229?
hints: He was born in Montpellier in 1208.
Years later he also conquered Valencia.
His nickname describes exactly what he did to Majorca.
questions.fun_fact: The white castle on a purple background on the Balearic flag comes from the flag of the city of Palma.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de

questions.description: It doesn't come in a carton, but it's served at concerts, matches and birthday parties.
questions.question: In Spain, if someone says a concert “ha sido la leche”, what do they mean it was?
hints: It's a very casual expression you hear a lot from young people.
It's like saying it was “una pasada”.
It's the opposite of saying it was “un rollo”.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Eres la leche!” can be said both to someone who leaves you speechless and to someone who drives you crazy.

media.credit: PinkBeachPlanet · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PinkBeachPlanet

questions.description: A little zippered house where nobody pays rent.
questions.question: It closes with a zipper, goes in your backpack and you open it in class. What's usually inside a pencil case?
hints: You need it to write and draw.
If you make a mistake, you take something out of here to fix it.
What's inside writes, rubs out and sharpens.
questions.fun_fact: Before erasers existed, people rubbed out pencil marks with soft bread.

media.credit: Dominique Roger · CC BY-SA 3.0 igo · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dominique Roger

questions.description: A tiny word that people in Spain throw out like a protective shield.
questions.question: In Spain, when do people usually say “¡Jesús!” to someone?
wrong_answers: Right after they blow out candles
hints: It's a very old custom of good manners.
It happens a lot when someone has a cold.
Just before it, you hear an “aaachoo!”.
questions.fun_fact: Some people keep count: “Jesús” for the first sneeze, “María” for the second, and “y José” for the third.

media.credit: family of Infrogmation of New Orleans · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: family of Infrogmation of New Orleans

questions.description: Some news leaves you speechless, and then you have to find a word anyway.
questions.question: You hear some unbelievable gossip and, jaw on the floor, blurt out a Spanish phrase you could also say about a bodybuilder. Which one?
hints: It shows surprise or outrage.
It has nothing to do with being bored or having a nerve.
A bodybuilder lifts lots of heavy weights.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Qué fuerte!” works for amazing news and for terrible news alike: it all depends on your tone of voice.

media.credit: Jamie McCaffrey · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jamie McCaffrey

questions.description: Every group of friends has one, and almost nobody volunteers for the role.
questions.question: In Spanish slang, this person always gets the job nobody wants and falls for every prank. Literally, the word means “smeared with grease.” What is it?
hints: It's the opposite of someone clever who always gets out of things.
It comes from a verb used for dipping bread in sauce.
If you get oil all over your clothes in Spain, you say «me he…»
questions.fun_fact: «Pringar» first meant dipping bread in grease; later it came to mean getting stuck with the dirty work or getting into a mess.

media.credit: Unidentified · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unidentified

questions.description: An actor who can go from grumpy father-in-law to philosopher in a single career.
questions.question: I was born in Vitoria, played Miguel de Unamuno in “Mientras dure la guerra” and was Koldo, Amaia's father, in “Ocho apellidos vascos”. Who am I?
hints: I'm Basque, from Álava.
I won the Goya for Best Supporting Actor for “Ocho apellidos vascos”, and before that for “También la lluvia”.
My first name starts with K.
questions.fun_fact: Karra Elejalde was nominated for the Goya for Best Actor for playing Unamuno in “Mientras dure la guerra”.

media.credit: Krzysztof Golik · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Krzysztof Golik

questions.description: A racer with a pilot's name: not quite the same job, but pretty close.
questions.question: Motorcycle racer Maverick Viñales is named after a fighter pilot from a movie. Which one?
hints: It's a movie from the 1980s.
Its star was Tom Cruise.
In 2022 it got a sequel named after the same pilot.
questions.fun_fact: Maverick Viñales was the Moto3 world champion in 2013.

media.credit: Liauzh · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Liauzh

questions.description: The upside of being the little brother: there's always someone to chase around the track.
questions.question: Àlex Márquez won Moto3 in 2014 and Moto2 in 2019, and his older brother is a MotoGP champion. In which Spanish region was he born?
hints: The region has a Mediterranean coastline.
The region borders France.
Its capital is Barcelona.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019 both Márquez brothers became world champions in the same year: Marc in MotoGP and Àlex in Moto2.

media.credit: Jmanall · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jmanall

questions.description: In this family you don't just inherit the name, you inherit a right foot glued to the accelerator.
questions.question: I'm a Formula 1 driver born in Madrid, named after my father, who won the Dakar several times and two World Rally titles. Who am I?
hints: People call me “Smooth Operator.”
I drove for Ferrari from 2021 to 2024.
My father is nicknamed “El Matador.”
questions.fun_fact: His first Formula 1 win came at the 2022 British Grand Prix at Silverstone.

media.credit: Sports Cars Fan · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sports Cars Fan

questions.description: A city where the ball gets bounced, not just kicked.
questions.question: Its basketball team won the EuroLeague in 2003 and 2010, and Pau Gasol and Juan Carlos Navarro played there. Which city is it from?
hints: It's a city on the Mediterranean Sea.
Its soccer club shares its name and colors with the basketball team.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.fun_fact: Barça won the 2003 EuroLeague at home, in the Final Four played at the Palau Sant Jordi.

media.credit: Wikideas1 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wikideas1

questions.description: The sport that has turned Sunday mornings into a sacred date.
questions.question: I was born in 1969 at a house in Acapulco, Mexico, and a prince brought me to Marbella in the 1970s. Which sport am I?
hints: I'm almost always played in pairs.
My court is surrounded by walls, and the ball can bounce off them.
I'm played with a pala, not a strung racket.
questions.fun_fact: Padel was invented by Enrique Corcuera at his home in Acapulco, and Alfonso de Hohenlohe brought it to the Marbella Club.

media.credit: Sally from Willamette Valley - Oregon, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sally from Willamette Valley - Oregon, USA

questions.description: Spain's big book of sayings has a very clear opinion about spring.
questions.question: It's April and you're heading out. According to the saying “En abril, aguas mil”, which of these will you NOT need?
hints: The saying is about the weather.
“Aguas mil” means a whole lot of rain.
Three of these things keep you from getting wet.
questions.fun_fact: Some people make it longer: “En abril, aguas mil, y todas caben en un barril” (and they all fit in a barrel), because some years it hardly rains.

media.credit: KaiBorgeest · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: KaiBorgeest

questions.description: The neighbors on the fifth floor know it better than they know the people on the fourth.
questions.question: In a Spanish apartment building, what is the “portero automático”?
questions.answer: The device to open the street door from home
wrong_answers: A guard who watches the entrance at night
A door that opens by itself as you approach
A mailbox that tells you when a letter arrives
hints: Almost every apartment building has one next to the entrance.
It rings when someone presses a button down on the street.
You pick up, ask “¿quién es?” and press the button with the key on it.
questions.fun_fact: In many new buildings the portero automático now has a camera, so you can see who's calling before you open.

media.credit: August Geyler · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: August Geyler

questions.description: Summer vacation officially starts when the trunk won't close anymore.
questions.question: I have plots, shared showers, camper vans and tents, and in summer I fill up with families. What am I?
hints: At night you hear crickets and zippers.
You sleep there almost in the open air.
In Spain, people call me by an English word for an outdoor activity.
questions.fun_fact: In English “camping” is the activity and the place is a “campsite”, but in Spain people say «un camping» for the place itself.

media.credit: Mhlayson · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mhlayson

questions.description: It has more lights than a Christmas tree, and it isn't even Christmas.
questions.question: I glow green on the front of a building, I have four equal arms, and sometimes I tell you the time and temperature. What am I?
hints: You see me in almost every neighborhood in Spain.
Under me, they sell cough syrup and bandages.
The people who work under my light wear white coats and hand out medicine.
questions.fun_fact: Many pharmacy crosses in Spain are LED screens that show pictures, the time and the temperature.

media.credit: Filip Trefil · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Filip Trefil

questions.description: The comfiest clothes in your closet, after your pajamas.
questions.question: Today you go to school in a chándal (tracksuit) instead of your usual clothes. What day is it most likely?
wrong_answers: The day of the class photo
The day of the Christmas show
hints: You're going to sweat a bit that day.
That day you need comfy sneakers and maybe a water bottle.
That day there are races, balls and jumping.
questions.fun_fact: “Chándal” comes from the French “marchand d'ail”, “garlic seller”, after the warm clothes those sellers wore.

media.credit: Brooke Fishwick · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Brooke Fishwick

questions.description: A doctor named after a piece of bedroom furniture.
questions.question: In Spain, what kind of doctor is the “médico de cabecera”?
questions.answer: The family doctor at your health center
wrong_answers: The surgeon in the operating room
hints: You're assigned one, and they often know your whole family.
If you feel unwell, they're the first one you book to see.
They send you to a specialist if needed.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “de cabecera” (of the headboard) because doctors once visited the sick at home and treated them at the head of the bed.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Goodbye playdough on the table, hello graph-paper notebooks.
questions.question: You're 5 and in the last year of Educación Infantil. Which school stage do you move up to next year?
hints: It's the stage where you fully learn to read and write.
It lasts six school years.
Its first year is called “primero de …”.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, Educación Infantil isn't compulsory, but almost all children aged 3 to 6 go to school anyway.

media.credit: Kgbo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kgbo

questions.description: A tradition that leaves birthday kids with ears as red as tomatoes.
questions.question: By Spanish custom, how many ear tugs do you get on your birthday?
questions.answer: One for each year you turn
wrong_answers: One for each guest at the party
hints: It happens once a year, and the birthday kid doesn't get to choose.
The number changes from one birthday to the next.
You count them just like the candles on the cake.
questions.fun_fact: Many people finish with one extra tug “so you'll grow”.

media.credit: Abinayasekar357 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Abinayasekar357

questions.description: The school subject where getting your hands dirty isn't a problem, it's the plan.
questions.question: You use tempera paints, scissors, glue and card stock to make murals and drawings. Which school subject is it?

TV in Spain still had very few channels.
It started a few years before Spain became a democracy.
questions.fun_fact: To Miliki's question, the children all answered at once with a very long “¡Bieeen!” (“Great!”).

media.credit: Ejegg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ejegg

questions.description: A neighborhood so old its stones are already collecting a pension.
questions.question: Pieces of the Roman city wall still stand in Barcelona's Gothic Quarter. Roughly how old are they?
hints: It's older than the name “Gothic” itself.
Back then, Barcelona was called Barcino.
It was built when the Roman Empire ruled Hispania, around the start of the Common Era.
questions.fun_fact: The famous Gothic bridge on Carrer del Bisbe looks medieval, but it was built in 1928.

media.credit: Tevfik Teker · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tevfik Teker

questions.description: The most exclusive retreat in Extremadura: no Wi-Fi, but plenty of monks.
questions.question: An emperor who had ruled half the world spent his last years in this monastery of Yuste, in Cáceres. Who was he?
hints: He was King of Spain and Holy Roman Emperor.
He was the grandson of the Catholic Monarchs.
As Holy Roman Emperor he carried a different number: V.
questions.fun_fact: Charles I loved clocks and took a whole collection of them with him to Yuste.

media.credit: José Luis Filpo Cabana · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Luis Filpo Cabana

questions.description: A concrete sculpture that stares at the sea like someone waiting for the bus.
questions.question: This large sculpture by Chillida, the “Elogio del Horizonte,” crowns a hill by the sea. Which city is it in?
hints: It's in northern Spain, facing the Cantabrian Sea.
It's the biggest city in its autonomous community, but not the capital.
It has San Lorenzo beach and the Cimadevilla neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: If you stand in the middle, under the sculpture, the concrete amplifies the sound of the wind and the waves.

media.credit: Zarateman · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zarateman

questions.description: A house with so many rooms that a game of hide-and-seek could last for years.
questions.question: Look at the photo: which building in Madrid is this?
hints: It stands next to the Almudena Cathedral.
It is used for official ceremonies of the head of state.
It is the king's official residence, though he doesn't live there.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Palace has more than 3,000 rooms and is the largest royal palace in Western Europe.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A street with “great” in its name… but how great is it in steps?
questions.question: Roughly how long is Madrid's Gran Vía from one end to the other?
hints: You can walk it without getting very tired.
It runs from Calle de Alcalá to Plaza de España.
At a relaxed pace, you can walk it in 15 to 20 minutes.
questions.fun_fact: The Telefónica Building on the Gran Vía was one of the first skyscrapers in Europe when it opened in 1929.

media.credit: Nan Palmero from San Antonio, TX, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nan Palmero from San Antonio, TX, USA

questions.description: Coming up with names for a city's residents: clearly a job for someone with a lot of imagination.
questions.question: In Spanish, what do you call someone born in the city of this basilica?
hints: The basilica stands by the Ebro River.
The city is the capital of Aragon.
It's the Basílica del Pilar.
questions.fun_fact: During the Fiestas del Pilar, thousands of people bring flowers to the Virgin, forming a huge floral cloak.

media.credit: de:Benutzer:Gisbertn · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: de:Benutzer:Gisbertn

questions.description: A square so square it could do its geometry homework all by itself.
questions.question: This painted front faces a square in Madrid lined with arcades, with a king on horseback in the middle. Which square is it?
hints: It dates from the early 17th century.
At Christmas it fills with stalls selling nativity scene figures.
The bars around it sell fried squid sandwiches.
questions.fun_fact: Madrid's Plaza Mayor has 237 balconies looking onto the square.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: Beach umbrella, towel and an accent that's definitely not from Alicante.
questions.question: You're in Benidorm and almost all the foreign tourists you hear come from the same country. What nationality are most of them?
hints: They come from a European country.
To get there, they usually fly across the sea.
Their capital is London.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1950s, Mayor Pedro Zaragoza rode a Vespa all the way to Madrid to argue for allowing the bikini in Benidorm.

media.credit: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen)

questions.description: Every city has its favorite saint, and some throw it a huge party.
questions.question: San Fermín is to Pamplona as San Isidro is to…
hints: It's celebrated on May 15.
People dress up as chulapos and dance the chotis.
It's the capital of Spain.
questions.fun_fact: San Isidro was a farm worker, and during his fiesta people eat rosquillas “tontas” and “listas” (“silly” and “smart” doughnuts).

media.credit: Inés Para Editar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Inés Para Editar

questions.description: A sweet so hard your teeth need a vacation after Christmas.
questions.question: This hard turrón, made with whole almonds, is named after the city it comes from. Which city?
hints: It's a beach city on the Mediterranean.
It's in the Valencian Community.
Its soft neighbor is turrón de Jijona.
questions.fun_fact: Turrón de Alicante is the hard one and turrón de Jijona the soft one, and both are made in the same province.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tamorlan

questions.description: A city whose Christmas lights try to outshine the sun itself.
questions.question: It's the largest city in Galicia, faces the Cíes Islands and is famous for its huge Christmas lights. Which city is it?
hints: It lies by the sea, on an Atlantic ría (estuary).
It has one of the biggest fishing ports in Europe.
Its soccer team is Celta.
questions.fun_fact: In 2007, the British newspaper The Guardian named Rodas Beach, on the Cíes Islands, the best beach in the world.

media.credit: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez

questions.description: An aristocrat who describes himself with three adjectives, and none of them is “humble.”
questions.question: The Marqués de Bradomín, “ugly, Catholic and sentimental,” is the hero of the four “Sonatas.” Which writer created him?
hints: The “Sonatas” came out in the early 20th century, between 1902 and 1905.
Each of the four novels is named after a season of the year.
The same author invented the esperpento in “Luces de bohemia.”
questions.fun_fact: Valle-Inclán lost his left arm after a fight in a Madrid café in 1899, and from then on his long beard and single arm became his trademark.

media.credit: Andrés Suárez García · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andrés Suárez García

questions.description: History's first boss to train his intern with knocks on the head.
questions.question: I was the first master of a boy born in the river Tormes. In Salamanca I banged his head against a stone bull, and he got back at me with a post. Who am I?
hints: I'm a character in “Lazarillo de Tormes”.
I made my living saying prayers in exchange for coins.
The boy led me through the streets because I couldn't see.
questions.fun_fact: The stone bull from the story still exists: it's an ancient Vettonian boar-bull statue kept next to Salamanca's Roman bridge.

media.credit: muffinn from Worcester, UK · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: muffinn from Worcester, UK

questions.description: A man from Seville who wrote about rogues and ended up packing his bags for the other side of the ocean.
questions.question: I was born in Seville in 1547. In 1599 I published the life of a rogue that was read all over Europe, and in 1608 I sailed to Mexico. Who am I?
hints: My novel came out a few years before Don Quixote.
In Mexico I also published a book on Spanish spelling.
My rogue was called Guzmán de Alfarache.
questions.fun_fact: His novel was such a hit that people simply called it “el Pícaro” (the Rogue), and a fake second part came out before the real one, just as would later happen to Don Quixote.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.description: A knight so famous that even his horse and his sword have names of their own.
questions.question: His name was Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, he rode Babieca, and he is buried in his home city's cathedral. Which city was El Cid from?
hints: It is a city in northern Castile.
Its Gothic cathedral is one of the most famous in Spain.
It is in Castile and León, and its name starts with B.
questions.fun_fact: “Cid” comes from the Arabic “sidi”, meaning “lord”, and even his enemies called him that.

media.credit: Søren Niedziella from Denmark · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Søren Niedziella from Denmark

questions.description: A poem with more sails, cannons and freedom than a pirate theme park.
questions.question: The “Canción del pirata” begins “Con diez cañones por banda, viento en popa a toda vela…” (“Ten cannons on each side, full sail before the wind…”). Who wrote it?
hints: He was a poet of Spanish Romanticism.
He was a rebel who spent years in exile and wrote “El estudiante de Salamanca”.
His surname starts with E.
questions.fun_fact: The pirate in the poem sings that his ship is called “el Temido” (“the Feared One”) and that his only god is freedom.

media.credit: Samuel Walters · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Samuel Walters

questions.description: A university rector who proved that you can lose the fight and still win the speech.
questions.question: In 1936, at the University of Salamanca, its rector stood up to General Millán Astray: “Venceréis, pero no convenceréis” (“You will win, but you won't convince”). Who was he?
hints: He was a Basque writer of the Generation of '98.
He wrote “Niebla,” where a character goes to argue with his own author.
He also wrote “San Manuel Bueno, mártir.”
questions.fun_fact: Unamuno was rector of the University of Salamanca several times, and you can still visit his house-museum next to the university today.

media.credit: Björn S. · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Björn S.

questions.description: The most romantic answer ever given to an exam question.
questions.question: “What is poetry?, you ask, as you fix your blue pupil on mine. […] Poetry… is you.” Who wrote these lines?
hints: He is a Romantic poet of the 19th century.
He also wrote spooky legends like “El monte de las ánimas” (“The Mount of Souls”).
He was from Seville and is also famous for “Volverán las oscuras golondrinas” (“The dark swallows will return”).
questions.fun_fact: Bécquer never saw his “Rimas” published as a book: his friends collected and published them in 1871, a year after his death.

media.credit: Ketter1 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ketter1

questions.description: A hat so elegant it wasn't happy staying inside a book.
questions.question: Pedro Antonio de Alarcón's novel “El sombrero de tres picos” (1874) became what in 1919?
questions.answer: A ballet with music by Falla
wrong_answers: An opera with music by Verdi
A zarzuela with music by Chapí
hints: It premiered in London with a famous Russian company.
The composer was from Cádiz and also wrote “El amor brujo.”
Picasso designed the sets and costumes, and there is dancing in it.
questions.fun_fact: Picasso designed the sets and costumes for the ballet, which was premiered by Diaghilev's Ballets Russes.

media.credit: Elliott Brown from Birmingham, United Kingdom · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Elliott Brown from Birmingham, United Kingdom

questions.description: The only place where dressing as a ninja with blue hair doesn't turn any heads.
questions.question: Spain's biggest manga and anime convention started in 1995 and is run by Ficomic. In which city is it held?
hints: It's a city on the Mediterranean Sea.
The same organizers hold the big comics convention there every spring.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.fun_fact: The Barcelona manga convention draws more than 150,000 visitors every year, many of them dressed as their favorite characters.

media.credit: istolethetv · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: istolethetv

questions.description: The best cure for “Are we there yet?” in the back seat of the car.
questions.question: It's a short text, often rhyming, that describes something without saying its name so you can guess it. What is it called?
hints: Kids play it a lot at school and on car trips.
At the end, someone always asks “What am I?”
Many start with “What has…”, like “What has keys but can't open locks?”
questions.fun_fact: Riddles are so old they already appear in Greek myths, like the famous riddle of the Sphinx.

media.credit: Nirmal Dulal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nirmal Dulal

questions.description: A neighborhood pickpocket with more bar-stool philosophy than money in his pocket.
questions.question: Which cartoonist created Makinavaja, “el último choriso” (the last petty crook), in the magazine El Jueves?
hints: He was Catalan and died in 1993.
His real name was Ramón Tosas.
His pen name has only three letters and an accent.
questions.fun_fact: Makinavaja reached the movies in 1992, played by Andrés Pajares.

media.credit: Daria · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daria

questions.description: Some looks say it all, and according to Grandma, some say far too much.
questions.question: People say it's cast just by looking, without touching, and that babies are the most at risk. In folk belief, what is the mal de ojo?
questions.answer: Bad luck caused by an envious look
wrong_answers: An infection caught by looking at someone
A punishment for spying on the neighbors
An illness from staring at the sun
hints: People use charms like the higa or a red ribbon to protect against it.
It's a superstition about bad luck, not a disease of the eyes or the body.
It's as if jealousy could bring bad luck.
questions.fun_fact: In Galicia, babies are traditionally given a higa made of jet to protect them from the mal de ojo.

media.credit: Hu Nhu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hu Nhu

questions.description: A boy who got lost and ended up in the coziest spot in the barn.
questions.question: Which fairy-tale character sings “I'm in the ox's belly, where it doesn't snow or rain”?
hints: He's so tiny that his family couldn't find him.
He walked down the street singing so nobody would step on him.
He's named after the legume that stars in cocido stew.
questions.fun_fact: In 1945, “Garbancito de la Mancha” came out; it's considered Europe's first full-length animated film in color.

media.credit: Józef Brodowski the Elder · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Józef Brodowski the Elder

questions.description: Get ready for the most annoying question of the afternoon, and not because it's hard.
questions.question: What is the name of the story that never ends, used to tease children?
hints: Parents and grandparents in Spain have played it with children for generations.
It starts with “¿Quieres que te cuente…?” (“Do you want me to tell you…?”).
Its name has something in it that you snack on in the park, from a sunflower.
questions.fun_fact: The trick is to answer every reply with “I didn't ask you to say yes, I asked if you want me to tell you the cuento de la buena pipa.”

media.credit: Ldorfman · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ldorfman

questions.description: A place with weather so nice that even the ancients gave it five stars.
questions.question: I'm a group of volcanic islands in the Atlantic, off the coast of Africa. Greeks and Romans said life on me was free of sorrow. What did they call me?
hints: Today I'm one of Spain's autonomous communities.
My highest peak is the Teide.
My ancient name is about good luck.
questions.fun_fact: Pityusic and Gymnesian were Greek names for the Balearic Islands: the first for Ibiza and Formentera, the second for Mallorca and Menorca.

media.credit: Ingo Mehling · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ingo Mehling

questions.description: The life of a cat with more drama than all nine lives put together.
questions.question: You're singing “Estaba el señor don Gato”. Which of these does NOT happen in the song?
wrong_answers: He comes back to life when he smells fish
hints: Something sad happens, but it ends well.
At the end, the funeral passes through the fish market street.
Don Gato doesn't catch anything in the whole song.
questions.fun_fact: “Don Gato” is an old ballad that has been sung in Spain for centuries, and in many countries of the Americas too.

media.credit: MichalPL · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MichalPL

questions.description: Neighbors who throw their parties in a cave and never invite anyone.
questions.question: They meet at night at the aquelarre, brew potions in a cauldron, and the Zugarramurdi cave is their most famous spot. Who are they?
hints: They often wear a pointy hat.
They fly around on a broomstick.
A very famous one gave Snow White a poisoned apple.
questions.fun_fact: In Zugarramurdi, in Navarre, there is a Witches' Museum very close to the famous cave.

media.credit: Eneko Bidegain · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eneko Bidegain

questions.description: A farmhouse neighbor who never pays the building fees.
questions.question: In Basque legends they call me iratxo, and I roam at night near the farmhouses. What am I?
hints: I'm small and not very harmful.
I love playing pranks and messing everything up.
I'm related to the trasgo of other regions.
questions.fun_fact: In Basque mythology, the pagan giants are the jentilak, the witches are the sorginak and the dragon is the herensuge.

media.credit: Wikimaribarre · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wikimaribarre

questions.description: Galicia's first builders, and they never asked for a building permit.
questions.question: Galician tradition says they live underground, guard treasures and built the castros (hillforts) and mámoas (burial mounds). Who are they?
hints: Almost anything ancient of unknown origin was credited to them.
Their enchanted women comb their hair beside springs.
Their name sounds almost like the Spanish word “moros” (Moors).
questions.fun_fact: Despite the name, the mouros of legend aren't Muslims: they're a magical people from a very distant past.

media.credit: kilezz/QuiRóH · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: kilezz/QuiRóH

questions.description: Even patron saints have a favorite home region.
questions.question: Our Lady of Covadonga is to Asturias as Our Lady of Montserrat is to…
hints: Her shrine sits on a mountain of strangely shaped rocks.
Her monastery has a famous boys' choir, the Escolanía.
People fondly call her “la Moreneta”, and her mountain is near Barcelona.
questions.fun_fact: The Escolanía de Montserrat is one of the oldest boys' choirs in Europe, with more than 700 years of history.

media.credit: Luis Fermín TURIEL PEREDO · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Fermín TURIEL PEREDO

questions.description: The only mouse that's welcome in the house.
questions.question: Why does Ratoncito Pérez come to children's homes?
questions.answer: To swap a baby tooth for a gift
wrong_answers: To eat the crumbs in the kitchen
hints: He comes when something happens in a child's mouth.
He looks under the pillow.
One falls out and you save it for him.
questions.fun_fact: Father Luis Coloma invented him in 1894 for the young King Alfonso XIII, and on Calle del Arenal in Madrid there's a plaque where he “lived”.

media.credit: Ahunt · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ahunt

questions.description: Shepherds, sheep and a river of tinfoil: the smallest town in all of Spain.
questions.question: They go in the belén (nativity scene), they're sold at the Christmas market in Madrid's Plaza Mayor, and the classic ones are hand-painted. What are they usually made of?
hints: It's a material that comes from the earth.
Before they're painted, they're baked in a kiln.
It's the same wet earth used to make botijos and water jugs.
questions.fun_fact: The nativity scene Francisco Salzillo made in Murcia in the 18th century has more than 500 figures.

media.credit: Javier Perez Montes · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Javier Perez Montes

questions.description: Recess always ends sooner than it takes to decide what to play.
questions.question: One player counts facing the wall while the others look for a good spot where they won't be seen. What game is it?
hints: Behind a curtain or under the bed is a good spot.
The one who counted then has to find everyone else.
At the end of the count, someone shouts “Ready or not, here I come!”
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, a player who reaches the base without being caught shouts “¡Por mí y por todos mis compañeros!” to free everyone.

media.credit: Unidentified · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unidentified

questions.description: A game where standing as still as a statue is the best plan.
questions.question: In “escondite inglés”, the player who is “it” turns around and shouts “Un, dos, tres…”. How does it go on?
hints: It's a small animal.
It's the baby of a farm bird.
Its mother is the hen.
questions.fun_fact: In England this game is called “Grandmother's Footsteps”.

media.credit: 玄史生 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: 玄史生

questions.description: The only race where hopping your way to the finish is completely normal.
questions.question: At Spanish village fiestas, people race like this. What fabric are these sacks traditionally made of?
hints: It's a rough, cheap fabric.
It's a little itchy and lets air through.
It's what potato sacks have always been made of.
questions.fun_fact: In many villages the sack race shares the fiesta program with the greasy pole and tug-of-war.

media.credit: Irsam Soetarto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Irsam Soetarto

questions.description: A two-person race where everything comes down to who has the faster reflexes.
questions.question: Two teams in rows, each player with a number. The person in the middle calls a number, and the two players with it race to grab… what?
hints: The person in the middle holds it out at arm's length.
Years ago almost everyone carried one every day.
You can also blow your nose with it.
questions.fun_fact: If you step over the center line before the other player grabs the object, you're out.

media.credit: Rodrigo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rodrigo

questions.description: A needle that got tired of being straight and decided to become a fishhook.
questions.question: What is this hook-tipped needle used for?
hints: Grandmothers used to do this a lot.
The hook catches the thread and makes loops.
It makes the doilies that sit on top of the mesa camilla (a round table with a heater underneath).
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word “ganchillo” comes from “gancho” (hook), after the curved tip of the needle.

media.credit: Jacek Halicki · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jacek Halicki

questions.description: For when a Sunday afternoon drags on longer than the line at the doctor's.
questions.question: You draw me with two lines standing up and two lying down. One player draws X's, the other O's, and three in a row wins. What game am I?
hints: I have nine squares.
Only two people play.
My name is three short words joined by hyphens.
questions.fun_fact: If neither player ever makes a mistake, the game always ends in a draw.

media.credit: John Phelan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Phelan

questions.description: A coffee that decided breakfast was too small for it.
questions.question: Mix orujo (a strong grape spirit) with coffee and sugar and you get licor café. Which region of Spain is it typical of?
hints: It's a very rainy land in the northwest.
Queimada is also made there with orujo.
Its capital is Santiago de Compostela.
questions.fun_fact: At Galician festivals it's common to end the meal with a shot of licor café, as dark as coffee itself.

media.credit: Ragesoss · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ragesoss

questions.description: At a Spanish bar counter, ordering is almost a language of its own.
questions.question: In a bar in Spain, what happens if you order a «jarra» of beer instead of a «caña»?
questions.answer: You get more, in a big glass with a handle
wrong_answers: You get less, in a small glass
You get it mixed with lemon
hints: It has to do with the amount.
You hold the glass in a special way.
It usually holds about half a liter.
questions.fun_fact: Depending on the bar and the city, a caña can be around 200 ml (7 fl oz), while a jarra is usually over half a liter.

media.credit: David Adam Kess · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Adam Kess

questions.description: A star you've never seen through a telescope, but you've seen it on plenty of café terraces.
questions.question: In which city was Estrella Damm beer born in 1876?
hints: It's a big city with an important port.
Its founder came from Alsace, in France.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.fun_fact: Estrella Galicia, from A Coruña, has nothing to do with Estrella Damm, even though both have the word “Estrella” in their names.

media.credit: Acabashi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Acabashi

questions.description: A pot with a hole in its head, and not because it's absent-minded.
questions.question: Old Spanish chocolate pots were tall and narrow, with a hole in the lid. What was that hole for?
questions.answer: To fit a wooden whisk for frothing
wrong_answers: To add milk without opening it
hints: A wooden stick went through it.
It was spun between the hands to make foam.
In Spain this tool is called a “molinillo”, like a small coffee mill.
questions.fun_fact: In the 17th and 18th centuries, drinking frothy chocolate was a fashion among the Spanish nobility.

media.credit: CNEcija12345 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: CNEcija12345

questions.description: The shortest dance routine at any Spanish party.
questions.question: Finish the classic Spanish toast: «Arriba, abajo, al centro y…»
hints: You say it while moving your glass.
It's the last thing you do with the drink.
It tells you where the drink ends up: in your mouth.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain it's also customary to look each other in the eye when toasting and say «¡Chinchín!» as the glasses clink.

media.credit: Dheera Venkatraman · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dheera Venkatraman

questions.description: Round orange balls that get squeezed and never complain.
questions.question: Fruit like the one in the photo is squeezed into fresh juice for breakfast. Which Spanish region is famous for it?
hints: It's in the east of the peninsula.
It has three provinces and two official languages.
Its capital has the same name as the region.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is one of the biggest orange exporters in the world.

media.credit: Ivar Leidus · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ivar Leidus

questions.description: Here you pay in euros, but everyone acts as if phones had never been invented.
questions.question: You stroll through a medieval market among costumed blacksmiths, falconers and minstrels. Which era came right after the one they imitate?
hints: The era they imitate is the age of castles and knights.
It began around the time Columbus reached the Americas.
It's the age of the printing press, the Renaissance and the great voyages of discovery.
questions.fun_fact: The Middle Ages lasted about a thousand years, from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 to the late 15th century.

media.credit: Croquettedejamon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Croquettedejamon

questions.description: The one day of the year when checking your back is a matter of survival.

questions.fun_fact: Legend says Abbot Saint Virila stopped to listen to a bird in the Leyre woods, and when he got back, 300 years had passed.

It's long, and its crust is crunchy.
You ask for “una…” and sometimes carry it home under your arm.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, people often buy fresh bread every day, and the barra is the best-selling bread.

media.author: Andy Li

questions.description: The moment on Sunday when you eat before you eat.
questions.question: It comes before lunch, it's often a vermouth with olives, and its name comes from the Latin “aperire”. What does that word mean?
hints: Think about what it's for, just before the meal.
It's meant to get your appetite going.
It's the opposite of “to close”.
questions.fun_fact: In many Spanish cities, going for “el vermut” on Sunday means the same as going out for an aperitivo.

media.credit: Kyle May · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kyle May

questions.description: Four sausages walk into a bar, and one of them is undercover.
questions.question: Which of these cured sausages does NOT contain pimentón?
hints: Look at the color of each one.
Pimentón dyes them red.
The one you're looking for has visible black peppercorns.
questions.fun_fact: Salchichón de Vic, from Catalonia, has Protected Geographical Indication status.

media.author: David Adam Kess

questions.description: A tiny shellfish that comes to the table in its own fancy can.
questions.question: This bivalve with a ridged shell is eaten from a can with lemon and gathered by hand in the rías at low tide. Which region has the most famous ones?
hints: It's on the Atlantic coast.
It's a region in the northwest, with lots of rain and lots of rías.
The Ría de Noia is one of its best-known spots.
questions.fun_fact: Cockles live buried in the sand and breathe through two little tubes that poke up to the surface.

media.credit: Alan Hughes · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alan Hughes

questions.description: A cool, dark cellar that grown-ups are never in a hurry to leave.
questions.question: You walk into a bodega in La Rioja and it smells of oak barrels. What is made there?
hints: It's made from fruit.
It's often left to age for years before it's sold.
It's made from grapes.
questions.fun_fact: “Bodega” comes from the Greek “apothēkē”, a storehouse, the same root as the English word “apothecary”.

media.credit: Michael Gaylard from Horsham, UK · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Gaylard from Horsham, UK

questions.description: A quiet town where, one weekend a year, nobody respects the speed limit.
questions.question: It opened in 1991, hosted the Spanish Formula 1 Grand Prix every year until 2025, and also hosts MotoGP. In which town is it?
hints: It's in Catalonia.
It's about 20 km (12 miles) from Barcelona, in the Vallès Oriental area.
Its name starts with “Mont”.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2026 the Spanish Grand Prix has been held in Madrid, and Montmeló still has its own race: the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix.

media.credit: William Murphy from Dublin, Ireland · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: William Murphy from Dublin, Ireland

questions.description: Three races, three jerseys, and a cyclist who dresses according to who's winning.
questions.question: Yellow is to the Tour de France as pink is to the Giro d'Italia, and … is to the Vuelta a España.
hints: It's the color worn by the leader of the overall standings.
The leader has worn it since 2010, the year Spain won the soccer World Cup.
It's the color of the Spanish national soccer team's shirt.
questions.fun_fact: Before red came back in 2010, the Vuelta leader wore yellow for a while, and later gold.

media.credit: Hullian111 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hullian111

questions.description: The indoor cousin that never has to worry about rain.
questions.question: In a futsal match, how many players from each team are on the court at once, counting the goalkeeper?
hints: Fewer than in the regular outdoor game.
Fewer than the seven players on a handball team.
You can count them on the fingers of one hand.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has won the Futsal World Cup twice, in 2000 and 2004.

media.credit: Hariboneagle927 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hariboneagle927

questions.description: Two Spaniards put on a ring you can't buy at any jewelry store.
questions.question: Look at the photo: in 2019, Marc Gasol and Serge Ibaka won the NBA title with this city's team. Which city is it?
hints: It's outside the United States.
It's the most populous city in Canada.
Its team is called the Raptors.
questions.fun_fact: Marc Gasol was the first player to win the NBA title and the Basketball World Cup in the same year: 2019.

media.credit: Taxiarchos228 · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Taxiarchos228

questions.description: A Hollywood team where the stars can dribble too.
questions.question: Complete: Pau Gasol won the NBA championship with the Los Angeles…
hints: They wear purple and gold.
Magic Johnson, Kobe Bryant and LeBron James played there.
The name comes from the many lakes of Minnesota, where the team began.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Lakers” comes from Minnesota, “the Land of 10,000 Lakes”: the team started in Minneapolis before moving to Los Angeles.

media.author: formulanone

questions.description: Hurrying without losing your cool: the Olympic version of being late for school.
questions.question: In race walking, where María Pérez and Álvaro Martín have been world champions, judges penalize “loss of contact”. What is it?
questions.answer: Having both feet off the ground
hints: It has to do with the feet and the ground.
It's exactly what separates walking from running.
One foot must always be touching the ground.
questions.fun_fact: At Paris 2024, María Pérez and Álvaro Martín won Olympic gold together in the mixed race walk relay.

media.credit: Bearas · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bearas

questions.description: A name over a hundred years old, with more trophies than shelves.

hints: It has to do with the club's history.
There's a crown on its crest.
It was granted by King Alfonso XIII.
questions.fun_fact: Many Spanish clubs have “Real” in their name for the same reason, like Real Sociedad and Real Betis.

media.author: Felipe Gabaldón

questions.description: A man from Madrid who spent half his life skidding along dirt roads, and got paid for it.
questions.question: In which decade did Carlos Sainz Sr. win his two World Rally Championships?
hints: He won them driving a Toyota.
The first came right at the start of the decade.
It was around the time Barcelona hosted the Olympic Games.
questions.fun_fact: He won his fourth Dakar in 2024, at 61, making him the oldest winner in the race's history.

media.author: Steven Harrell

questions.description: A racket that got tired of strings and filled itself with holes instead.
questions.question: Look at the photo: padel isn't played with a strung racket, but with this. What is it called in Spain?
hints: It's used with a ball much like a tennis ball.
It's a four-letter word.
On Spanish beaches, people play with wooden ones.
questions.fun_fact: Inside, many padel palas are filled with a foam called EVA, the same material found in the soles of many sneakers.

media.author: Anton Gustafsson

questions.description: A family man who has spent more than twenty years without ever leaving the TV.
questions.question: This actor played Antonio Alcántara in «Cuéntame cómo pasó». What is his name?
hints: He was born in the 1950s in a village in the mountains of León.
His wife in the series was Ana Duato, who played Merche.
His first name is the Basque form of “Manuel”.
questions.fun_fact: «Cuéntame cómo pasó» premiered in 2001 and is the series with the most seasons in Spanish TV history.

media.credit: Rastrojo (D•ES) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rastrojo (D•ES)

questions.description: A face more people have worn than sunglasses in August.
questions.question: He had a pointy mustache, painted melting clocks, and his face is the mask in “Money Heist”. Which region of Spain was he from?
hints: We're talking about the surrealist painter Salvador Dalí.
His theater-museum is in his hometown, Figueres.
It's the region whose capital is Barcelona.
questions.fun_fact: Dalí is buried under the dome of his own Theater-Museum in Figueres.

media.author: Brandie!

questions.description: A song that sticks to you worse than gum on the bottom of your shoe.
questions.question: In «La casa de papel» (Money Heist) they sing “O bella ciao, bella ciao, bella ciao, ciao, ciao.” What does “bella ciao” mean?
hints: The song is Italian.
The robbers sing it, and they see themselves as resistance fighters.
It's a farewell said to a girl.
questions.fun_fact: “Bella ciao” became famous as a song of the Italian partisans in World War II, and the show made it a hit all over the world again.

media.author: Annika of Nine

questions.description: A Madrid neighborhood where the hardware store sees more action than a Hollywood movie.

Before this, he starred in the Telecinco series «El Príncipe».
He won the Goya for Best Actor for «No Rest for the Wicked» («No habrá paz para los malvados»).
questions.fun_fact: Entrevías is a real neighborhood in the Puente de Vallecas district of Madrid.

media.credit: Ruben Ortega · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ruben Ortega

questions.description: A show where whole towns put their honor on the line in front of a young cow.
questions.question: Who is this host of the «Grand Prix del verano»?

On New Year's Eve he often hosted the midnight chimes wearing a cape.
His first name is the same as Ramón y Cajal's.
questions.fun_fact: The «Grand Prix» returned to TVE in 2023, almost twenty years after its last season.

questions.question: Sherlock Holmes is to Watson as Sandra, the Fairytale Detective, is to…

His name has only two letters and starts with F.
questions.fun_fact: “Sandra, the Fairytale Detective” is a Spanish cartoon series that aired in many countries.

media.author: Virginia Frances Sterret

I host “First Dates” on Cuatro.
questions.fun_fact: This quiz show format was born in the UK in 1998 and has aired in more than 100 countries.

media.author: Tim Johnson from Savannah, GA, USA

It's an animal that lives and hunts in a pack.
It's the animal that howls at the moon in fairy tales.
questions.fun_fact: The show's name copies the sound of the bomb that goes off when you get it wrong.

questions.description: Stones so huge that even the toughest moving company wouldn't dare touch them.
questions.question: You're inside a dolmen, like the ones at Antequera. Which of these is NOT true about it?
questions.answer: It was built to store grain
wrong_answers: It was usually a shared tomb
It is made of huge stone slabs
hints: Three of the sentences are true; look for the one that doesn't fit its purpose.
Inside dolmens, archaeologists have found bones and grave goods.
It was a place for the dead, not a storeroom.
questions.fun_fact: The Dolmen de Menga faces the Peña de los Enamorados, a mountain shaped like a face lying on its back.

media.author: Andrzej Otrębski

questions.description: The first graffiti in history, and nobody gave it a fine.
questions.question: In 1879, someone first spotted the bison painted on the ceiling of the Altamira cave. Who was it?
hints: It was someone who went into the cave with a family member.
A father was searching the floor of the cave for prehistoric remains and didn't look up.
Her name was María, and she was very young.
questions.fun_fact: As the story goes, María shouted “Look, Daddy, oxen!” when she saw the bison on the ceiling.

media.credit: Thomas Quine · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Quine

questions.description: The Romans left, but they forgot to take their dictionary with them.
questions.question: You're reading a newspaper in Spanish. Roughly how many of its words come from Latin?
hints: Spanish grew out of the Latin spoken in Roman Hispania.
It's a large majority.
More than 70%.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word «hablar» (to speak) comes from the Latin «fabulari», which meant to chat or tell stories.

media.credit: Luis Rogelio HM · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Rogelio HM

questions.question: This Iberian sculpture, the Lady of Baza, was found in Granada in 1971. In which museum is it shown today?
hints: It isn't in the province where it was found.
It's in Madrid.
It's the same museum that holds the Lady of Elche.
questions.fun_fact: The Lady of Baza was a funeral urn: it held the remains of a cremation inside.

media.author: Miguel Hermoso Cuesta

questions.description: Some sea snails that ended up dressing kings and emperors.
questions.question: On an Andalusian beach you find a murex shell, once used to make purple dye. Which people, whose Greek name came from that color, made the dye?
hints: They were great sailors and traders of the Mediterranean.
They came from cities like Tyre and Sidon, in today’s Lebanon.
They founded Gadir, today’s Cádiz.
questions.fun_fact: It took thousands of snails to dye a single tunic, which is why purple was the color of the powerful.

media.author: Judy Gallagher

questions.description: The biggest secret weapon ever seen around Soria.
questions.question: In 153 BC, the Roman consul Nobilior attacked Numantia with elephants. One was hit on the head by a stone. What happened?
questions.answer: The elephants panicked and trampled the Romans
wrong_answers: The Numantians surrendered when they saw the animals
The elephants knocked down Numantia’s walls
The Romans took the city that same day
hints: The elephants came from North Africa, sent by Masinissa, king of Numidia.
Think about how a huge animal reacts when something hurts.
The Romans ended up running away.
questions.fun_fact: Numantia held out against Rome for about 20 years, until Scipio surrounded it with a siege in 133 BC.

media.author: Javier Mediavilla Ezquibela

questions.description: Almost 2,000 years standing, and not one complaint about the damp Galician weather.
questions.question: Look at the Tower of Hercules in A Coruña. Why did the Romans build it?
hints: It stands by the sea.
The Romans shipped lots of goods along the Atlantic coast.
It helps sailors keep from crashing into the coast.
questions.fun_fact: It is the oldest Roman lighthouse in the world that still works, and it has been a World Heritage Site since 2009.

media.author: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez (Lmbuga)

Work on it began in 1751, when Ferdinand VI was already king.
In Spanish, its name means “cold river”.
questions.fun_fact: Alfonso XII shut himself away in this palace to mourn after the death of his young wife, María de las Mercedes.

media.credit: Mike Prince from Bangalore, India · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mike Prince from Bangalore, India

questions.description: A countess who liked the pen more than the crown.

Her most famous novel is set in a Galician manor house.
She wrote “The House of Ulloa”.
questions.fun_fact: She applied to the Royal Spanish Academy several times and was always turned down for being a woman.

hints: In Madrid he lived at the Residencia de Estudiantes.

He is famous for his melting clocks and his curled-up mustache.
questions.fun_fact: The Academy, founded in 1752 under Ferdinand VI, holds paintings by Goya, who was once one of its directors.

media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: A nickname you won't find on any greeting card.

hints: At first, the people called him “el Deseado” (the Desired One).
He swore to uphold the Constitution in 1820 and later abolished it.
It's someone who breaks their word and betrays those who trust them.
questions.fun_fact: He was called “el Deseado” because, during the war against Napoleon, he spent six years held in France while Spaniards waited for his return.

The Puerta de Alcalá was built during his reign.
He was the son of Felipe V and the half-brother of Fernando VI, whom he succeeded.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos III brought streetlamps, sewers and garbage collection to a Madrid where people threw their waste out the window.

It's the same year Napoleon invaded Russia.
questions.fun_fact: Today “¡viva la Pepa!” describes someone carefree, though it started out as a liberal battle cry.

media.author: Axel Cotón Gutiérrez

hints: He first ruled in Naples.
He took the throne after his half-brother died.
He was the Italian queen's first son.
questions.fun_fact: Elisabeth Farnese fought so hard for her sons that one became King of Spain and another Duke of Parma.

media.author: Zarateman

questions.description: A politician who turned government into a chore chart, like taking turns washing the dishes.

He was the main author of the 1876 Constitution.
His surname includes the Spanish word for a castle.

The odd one out comes from an older novel.
She is the lady Don Quixote falls in love with.

questions.description: A car with a vacation name, for driving to work while dreaming of the beach.

Turkey, chorizo and cooked ham.

questions.description: Losing recess is the worst news a soccer ball eager to play could ever get.

You see them every day in your classroom.
In Spain, kids call them «profe».
questions.fun_fact: Decades ago, in many schools a punished student was made to stand facing the wall in a corner of the classroom.

media.author: Greenestreetfs

questions.description: The place where your backpack weighs more on Monday than on Friday.

questions.description: A mailman, a toymaker and a studio that didn't need to travel to the North Pole to find Christmas.

hints: Before directing films, he drew comics.

His last name contains the Spanish word for “church”.
