hints: It's full of pine forests, deer, Spanish ibex and bearded vultures.
Its full name also includes the Sierra de Segura and Las Villas.
It shares its name with a Jaén town with a castle, and the name sounds a bit like «cazar» (to hunt).
questions.fun_fact: This natural park covers more than 200,000 hectares (about half a million acres), and bearded vultures breed there again.

media.credit: Urci dream · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Urci dream

questions.description: A lake that dyed itself bubble-gum pink without a trip to the hair salon.
questions.question: Next to the pink lagoon of Torrevieja there are white mountains that aren’t made of snow. What are they made of?
hints: The lagoon sits right next to the sea.
The sun and wind dry up the water and leave this on the ground.
You sprinkle it on your food, and too much makes you thirsty.
questions.fun_fact: The pink color comes from tiny algae and bacteria that live in very salty water.

media.credit: Thomas Dahlstrøm Nielsen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Dahlstrøm Nielsen

questions.description: Their office has trees instead of walls and birds instead of printers.
questions.question: They wear uniforms, drive off-road vehicles and can give fines. What is the main job of Spain’s forest rangers?
questions.answer: To watch over and protect the countryside
wrong_answers: To cut down trees and sell the wood
hints: Their work has to do with nature.
If they see smoke in the forest, they’re among the first to raise the alarm.
They make sure no one harms the forests or their animals.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, forest rangers are officers of the law, like the police, and can report anyone who damages the countryside.

media.credit: JopkeB · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JopkeB

questions.description: A collecting contest where every trading card is a whole landscape.
questions.question: Which Spanish autonomous community has the most national parks?
hints: It has four.
None of its national parks shares land with another community.
One of them is Teide.
questions.fun_fact: The four Canary Islands national parks are Teide, Timanfaya, Garajonay and Caldera de Taburiente.

media.credit: Trougnouf (Benoit Brummer) · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Trougnouf (Benoit Brummer)

questions.description: Neighbors who take very long vacations and always come back to the same bell tower.
questions.question: If you live in Trujillo, you hear the lesser kestrels at the church again when they return from Africa to breed. When is that?
hints: They arrive before many other migrating birds.
They want their chicks ready when there are lots of insects.
They come back while it's still cold, before spring begins.
questions.fun_fact: Lesser kestrels nest in colonies in gaps in roofs, churches and castles, and eat mostly grasshoppers.

media.credit: Discasto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Discasto

questions.description: Two sisters who skip the cheese but nibble up millions of views.
questions.question: Las Ratitas are two Spanish sisters, Gisele and Claudia, with millions of YouTube followers. What videos do they post?
hints: Most of their fans are very young.
They appear in the videos themselves, with costumes and surprises.
It's what kids do at recess, but on camera.
questions.fun_fact: Las Ratitas started making videos when they were very little, and theirs is one of the most-watched kids' channels in Spain.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: A wheel of numbers where Los 40, the SER and your favorite car station all live.
questions.question: On FM radio in Spain, as in almost every country, between which numbers do you tune in to stations?
hints: They are measured in megahertz.
There are about twenty units between the lowest and highest numbers.
The highest number is just over a hundred.
questions.fun_fact: FM stands for “frequency modulation”, and it sounds better than AM, though its waves don't travel as far.

media.credit: ja:User:Sanjo · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ja:User:Sanjo

questions.description: Tears, impossible love affairs and fake slamming doors… and half of Spain was hooked at the same hour.
questions.question: I was a hit in 1950s and '60s Spain: daily episodes, actors who only lent their voices, sound effects made by hand. My biggest hit was “Ama Rosa”. What am I?
hints: Families gathered around the set so as not to miss a single episode.
Horses and rain were imitated with coconut shells or crumpled paper.
I'm like a telenovela, but you listen to me.
questions.fun_fact: “Ama Rosa”, written by Guillermo Sautier Casaseca for Cadena SER, left the streets half empty while it was on the air.

media.credit: Russell Lee · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Russell Lee

questions.description: A station that keeps you company at breakfast, in traffic jams and on the way home.
questions.question: This radio network was founded in 1990 by ONCE, now belongs to Atresmedia and airs the show “Más de uno”. Which is it?
hints: It's a private station, not RTVE's public one.
It has the same owner as the TV channels Antena 3 and laSexta.
Its name includes the Spanish word for a number that means “nothing”.
questions.fun_fact: Onda Cero was formed in 1990 by merging stations ONCE had bought, such as those of the old Cadena Rato.

media.credit: M4th5 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: M4th5

questions.description: A dish so big you need the whole family around it to finish it.
questions.question: Look closely at this paella. What kind of paella is it?
hints: Take a good look at what's on top of the rice.
Look at the dark shells peeking out of the rice.
It has prawns, mussels and langoustines.
questions.fun_fact: For many people from Valencia, the original paella has no seafood at all, just chicken, rabbit and green beans.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tamorlan

questions.description: Little balls that have kept grandparents and grandkids happy for generations.
questions.question: Look at this photo. What is this dish called?
hints: They're made with ground meat, egg and bread.
They're cooked in a sauce that you mop up with bread.
Their name starts with “al-”, like many Spanish words that come from Arabic.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish bars, albóndigas are one of the most-ordered tapas, especially in tomato or almond sauce.

media.credit: Avicentegil · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Avicentegil

questions.description: That little plate in the middle of the table that friends fight over down to the last piece.
questions.question: Look at this tapa. What is it called?
hints: It's one of the most famous tapas in Spain.
You order it to share at the bar, pick it up with a toothpick, and every bar boasts about its own sauce.
Its name says these potatoes have a fierce temper.
questions.fun_fact: Brava sauce usually contains hot pimentón (paprika), and many bars boast about their own secret recipe.

media.credit: Krista · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Krista

questions.description: Two ingredients that met in a mortar and never split up again.
questions.question: It's a thick white sauce from Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands, served with black rice. What does its name, alioli, mean?
hints: Its name is two words joined together.
“Oli” sounds a bit like “oil”.
One of the ingredients is bought in heads and split into cloves.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional alioli is made just by crushing garlic in a mortar and slowly adding oil, with no egg at all.

media.credit: JArribasphoto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JArribasphoto

questions.description: An S that crossed the ocean and decided to stay for good.
questions.question: Latin American seseo, saying «casa» (house) just like «caza» (hunt), came mostly with settlers from one Spanish region. Which?
hints: It's a region in the south of the peninsula.
Ships bound for the Americas sailed from its ports.
You also hear «miarma» and «quillo» there.
questions.fun_fact: People in the Canary Islands use seseo too, and many ships heading to the Americas stopped there on the way.

media.credit: Hendrick Cornelisz Vroom · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hendrick Cornelisz Vroom

questions.description: What your mom makes you take “just in case”, even when the sun is blazing.
questions.question: In Spain, when rain is on the way, you often hear “coge el chubasquero”. What is a chubasquero?
hints: You use it when the weather turns bad.
A “chubasco” is a short, heavy shower.
It's a jacket that keeps the water out.
questions.fun_fact: Many chubasqueros fold up small enough to fit in a pouch the size of a fist.

media.credit: JIP · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JIP

questions.description: A word that says “loads” with hardly any letters.
questions.question: “Una pechá de gente” means “a whole lot of people”. In which region of Spain do you mostly hear this expression?
hints: People there are known for swallowing letters when they speak.
It's the region of Spain with the most people.
It's the region of Seville, Málaga and Granada.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish dictionary defines “pechada” as “hartazgo” (a bellyful), so “una pechá” is literally a bellyful.

media.credit: Frédérique Voisin-Demery from Grenoble, France · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Frédérique Voisin-Demery from Grenoble, France

questions.description: Someone who gets up even earlier than the tomatoes.
questions.question: I live by the Segura river, among irrigation ditches and lemon trees, and my way of speaking is called panocho. Who am I?
hints: I work the land in a fertile valley in southeast Spain.
My festival is held in Murcia just after Holy Week.
My name comes from the place where I grow my vegetables.
questions.fun_fact: During the Bando de la Huerta, Murcia fills with people wearing the traditional huertano costume.

media.credit: LBM1948 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: LBM1948

questions.description: A pet name that came straight out of the pond.
questions.question: In Spain, if a grown-up says to a child “¡Ven aquí, renacuajo!”, what is the child being called?
hints: It's an affectionate nickname.
A “renacuajo” is a baby frog: a tadpole.
It has to do with size.
questions.fun_fact: “Renacuajo” comes from “rana” (frog), and Spaniards also use it for a small person or a little kid.

media.credit: Dave Spicer · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dave Spicer

questions.description: Something with more names than a king.
questions.question: In Madrid or Catalonia they're called “bambas”, and elsewhere “tenis” or “playeras”. What are they?
hints: You wear them on your feet.
You wear them in gym class.
They're made for running and have laces.
questions.fun_fact: In many places they're called “tenis” because they first became popular for playing tennis.

media.credit: Mk2010 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mk2010

questions.description: A composer whose tunes reached more living rooms than most TV hosts.
questions.question: Antón García Abril, who wrote the music for the nature series “El hombre y la Tierra”, composed the official anthem of which Spanish region?
hints: It's an inland region with no coastline.
The region has three provinces.
García Abril was born in Teruel, and the Ebro River flows through this region.
questions.fun_fact: García Abril also wrote the theme tunes of TV series such as “Fortunata y Jacinta” and “Anillos de oro”.

media.credit: Gerarus · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gerarus

questions.description: An island so windy that even the dunes comb their own hair.
questions.question: You're on a beach on the east side of Fuerteventura, looking out to sea. Roughly how far away is the coast of Africa?
hints: It is the Canary Island closest to Africa.
A passenger plane would cross it in less than a quarter of an hour.
It's roughly two and a half marathons back to back.
questions.fun_fact: Calima, a haze of dust from the Sahara Desert, sometimes reaches Fuerteventura on the wind.

media.credit: Pittigrilli · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pittigrilli

They became Spain's first national park, in 1918.
Their name includes the name of a continent.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that they got their name because they were the first land sailors saw on their way back from the Americas.

media.credit: Parraguesu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Parraguesu

questions.description: A matching game played with the map of Spain's regions spread out on the table.

hints: We're looking for the region's capital.

The Camino, the famous pilgrims' route, ends there.
questions.fun_fact: Its cathedral has a giant incense burner, the botafumeiro, which weighs about 53 kg (117 lb) and swings from side to side.

media.credit: Jim Anzalone · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jim Anzalone

questions.description: Some people have too much to say to fit it all through one mouth.
questions.question: In Spain, someone who talks nonstop and never lets you get a word in “habla por los…” what?
hints: You have two of them.
They're on your arm.
You rest them on the table, even when you're told not to.
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese has the same saying: “falar pelos cotovelos”, which also means talking through your elbows.

media.credit: Nattes à chat · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nattes à chat

questions.description: A Spanish custom that leaves your face more greeted than a striker after a goal.

hints: It's a small number.
In some parts of France they give more than in Spain.
One on each cheek.
questions.fun_fact: In France the number of kisses depends on the region: two in some areas, three or even four in others.

It's the fortress of House Targaryen, and its name joins a rock with a fire-breathing beast.
questions.fun_fact: To reach the hermitage on Gaztelugatxe, you have to climb about 241 steps.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.question: I was born in Mahón, Menorca, in 1992, and became world number 1 in a paddle sport played in pairs inside glass walls. Who am I?
hints: My sport was born in Mexico and is a huge hit in Spain.
I'm the big Balearic star of women's padel.
My last name starts with “Tr”.
questions.fun_fact: Padel was invented by Enrique Corcuera at his home in Acapulco, Mexico, in 1969.

media.author: Samson Ssemakadde

It was around the time Spanish kids go back to school.
questions.fun_fact: The archer who lit the Olympic cauldron in Barcelona, Antonio Rebollo, was a Paralympic athlete.

media.author: Norman Bailey/Australian Paralympic Committee

hints: All four are in the north of the Iberian Peninsula.
Three of them have their own regional parliament and president within Spain.
It's in the Pyrenees and is an independent country.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the 17 communities, Spain has two autonomous cities: Ceuta and Melilla.

media.author: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen)

hints: Many big cities have one or more roads of this kind.

It loops all the way around the city center.
questions.fun_fact: Part of the M-30 runs through tunnels under the Madrid Río park, next to the Manzanares river.

hints: It is one of the biggest cities in Spain.
The Guadalquivir River flows through it.
The Giralda tower is there.
questions.fun_fact: Seville has a public bike rental service called Sevici, running since 2007.

media.author: Fabián Heredia Montiel

A covered stop where buses pick you up
A tunnel that goes through a mountain
hints: It's on the road, at ground level.
Many have gardens or statues in the middle.
Its shape is like a circle.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, the car already driving inside a rotonda (roundabout) has the right of way.

He is British and designed the London skyscraper nicknamed “the Gherkin”.
questions.fun_fact: Locals call these glass entrances “fosteritos” (little Fosters), after their architect.

media.author: Giorgio Galeotti

questions.description: A kitchen where the nerves sneak right into the frying pan.

hints: It's not the version where kids cook.
The contestants were already on TV before they joined.
The name includes a word for a famous person.

The city is on the Mediterranean coast.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.fun_fact: Jordi Cruz won his first Michelin star at 24, at the restaurant L'Estany Clar.

It also airs “La ruleta de la suerte” and “Pasapalabra”.
questions.fun_fact: Antena 3 started broadcasting on January 25, 1990, after some test broadcasts at Christmas 1989.

questions.description: A vacation on a tropical island where nobody wants to stay.

Without it, they only have rice and whatever they catch.
It could be a pizza or a sandwich.
questions.fun_fact: Many “Supervivientes” contestants leave the island several kilos lighter than when they arrived.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: The alarm goes off at six and you're already bargaining for five more minutes.
questions.question: You get up really early to do your homework. According to the Spanish saying, who helps those who rise early?
hints: In Spanish, the saying begins “A quien madruga…”.
He appears in lots of other Spanish sayings and expressions.
Many religions say he lives in heaven.
questions.fun_fact: Another Spanish saying argues the opposite: “No por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano” (getting up early won't make the sun rise sooner).

media.credit: Thomas Holbach · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Holbach

questions.question: Complete the Spanish comparison for someone who can't hear a thing: “Más sordo que una…” (deafer than a…)

There, the bell marked the end of each round.

media.author: Ansgar Koreng

They kept watch over their weapons before being dubbed with a sword.

They grumble, complain and slam doors.

media.author: emp&isd

It's where you live.

media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: The summer warning that has saved more sandwiches than swimmers.
questions.question: It's summer, you're at the town pool and you've just eaten. Many grandparents say if you jump in now, what can you get?

Spanish grandparents call it a “corte de…” something.

media.credit: Airman 1st Class Mozer Da Cunha · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Airman 1st Class Mozer Da Cunha

It's a classic at Nochebuena dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Spain's most famous turrón comes from Jijona, in Alicante, which even has a museum all about it.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: The piece of paper that travels from school to home slower than any other, especially if it holds surprises.

media.author: DimiTalen

questions.question: In «El pueblo», some city people move to Peñafría, a nearly empty village. What do people in Spain call the areas that lose people like this?
hints: The phrase is about people who have left.
It is often used for Soria, Teruel or inland Castile.
The name makes it sound as if someone had poured the people out of a container.
questions.fun_fact: The series was filmed in Valdelavilla, a hamlet in Soria that had had no permanent residents for decades.

media.credit: Esther Pérez Pérez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Esther Pérez Pérez

questions.description: Eight years with the keys to the Moncloa in his pocket.
questions.question: I was Prime Minister of Spain from 1996 to 2004: I came after Felipe González and Zapatero followed me. Who am I?
hints: I was leader of the Partido Popular.
While I was in office, euro coins and bills landed in people's pockets.
Before that, I led the regional government of Castilla y León.
questions.fun_fact: Before moving into the Moncloa, Aznar was president of Castilla y León from 1987 to 1989.

media.credit: Yeray Díaz Zbida from Melilla, España · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yeray Díaz Zbida from Melilla, España

questions.description: A tree that has watched Basque history go by for centuries.
questions.question: Guernica, the Basque town of this tree, was bombed on April 26, 1937. Who carried out the attack?
hints: They were foreign pilots helping one side in the war.
The attack was a test run for air tactics later used in World War II.
They were Franco’s allies, and they were named after a huge bird of the Andes.
questions.fun_fact: The oak tree standing in Gernika in 1937 survived the bombing.

media.credit: Lpikaza · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lpikaza

questions.description: The Romans' food container, with two handles and no plastic lid to lose.
questions.question: Look at this clay jar with two handles and a pointed base: the Romans filled it with wine, oil or garum. What is it called?
hints: It traveled in ships' holds all over the Mediterranean.
The pointed base let it be stuck in sand or wedged between others.
Its Greek name means “carried on both sides”, after its two handles.
questions.fun_fact: In Rome there is a hill, Monte Testaccio, made almost entirely of broken amphorae that carried olive oil from Hispania.

media.credit: CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: An elephant that refused to leave the house without its coat.
questions.question: Remains of woolly mammoths have been found in Padul (Granada). When did these hairy giants live in Spain?
hints: Their very long hair helped them survive terrible cold.
They lived alongside the first humans, who hunted them.
Back then, huge glaciers covered much of Europe.
questions.fun_fact: The Padul mammoths lived about 35,000 years ago and are among the southernmost found anywhere in Europe.

media.credit: HTO · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: HTO

questions.description: The liquid gold that Spaniards pour on everything, even breakfast.
questions.question: Look at these trees: in Roman Hispania, their oil was already shipped to Rome. Which Spanish region has the most of them today?
hints: The Romans called this area Baetica, after the Guadalquivir River.
It's in the south of Spain, where summers are very hot.
Jaén, one of its provinces, is famous for its seas of olive trees.
questions.fun_fact: The province of Jaén alone has more than 60 million olive trees.

media.credit: agracier - NO VIEWS · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: agracier - NO VIEWS

questions.description: A gift from Felipe V that, more than three centuries later, nobody has finished unwrapping.
questions.question: Felipe V founded it in 1712. It stands on Madrid's Paseo de Recoletos and keeps a copy of almost everything published in Spain. What is it?
hints: You don't go there to look at paintings, but to read and study.
It holds millions of books, maps, sheet music and newspapers.
It's the place with the most books in all of Spain.
questions.fun_fact: It shares its Recoletos building with the National Archaeological Museum.

media.credit: Hyacinthe Rigaud · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hyacinthe Rigaud

questions.description: Some people lose their temper; she just lost her patience with the French.
questions.question: In 1808 I defended Zaragoza from the French: when the gunners beside me fell, I grabbed the fuse and fired the cannon myself. Who am I?
hints: I'm a heroine of the Peninsular War.
Goya drew me next to a cannon in a print called “¡Qué valor!” (“What courage!”).
I'm known by the name of the region whose capital I defended.
questions.fun_fact: Although she is remembered for Zaragoza, Agustina was born in Barcelona in 1786.

media.credit: Willtron · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Willtron

questions.description: A revolt in which Madrid fashion said “enough is enough.”
questions.question: The 1766 Esquilache Riot, against a minister of Charles III, is also called the “riot of cloaks and…”. How does the name end?
hints: Esquilache didn't want people in Madrid to be able to hide their faces in the street.
The decree set how long a cloak could be, and it also went after something worn above it.
Along with the long cloak, the chambergo, a wide-brimmed one, was banned.
questions.fun_fact: Esquilache was Italian, from Sicily, and after the riot Charles III had to dismiss him.

media.credit: Carlos Delgado · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Delgado

questions.description: A neighbor so close you can see it from the window, but it asks for a different passport.
questions.question: Which of these places is NOT Spanish territory?
hints: It's in the south, very close to Africa.
People there pay in pounds, and cars have British license plates.
It has belonged to the United Kingdom since the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.
questions.fun_fact: Menorca was also British for much of the 18th century, until it went back to Spain in 1802.

media.credit: ד"ר אבישי טייכר · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ד"ר אבישי טייכר

questions.description: A city that sat down to write laws while surrounded by French cannons.
questions.question: The French besieged it from 1810 to 1812, members of parliament took refuge there and Spain's first constitution was born there. Which city is it?
hints: It is in the south of Spain.
It is nicknamed “la tacita de plata” (the little silver cup).
It is the city of chirigotas and Spain's most famous carnival.
questions.fun_fact: The Cortes (parliament) first met in nearby Isla de León, today San Fernando, and moved into the city in 1811.

media.credit: Creator:Martinus Nellius · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Creator:Martinus Nellius

questions.description: The First Republic had big plans and very little time to carry them out.
questions.question: The draft federal Constitution of 1873 split Spain into 17 states, such as Aragon or Catalonia. What for?
questions.answer: So each one would have its own government and laws
wrong_answers: So each one could choose its own king
To spread the army's barracks out better
So Madrid would have even more power
hints: It was a republic, so no kings at all.
Francisco Pi y Margall, one of its presidents, backed it.
Each state would have its own parliament, joined to a shared one for all of Spain.
questions.fun_fact: Cuba and Puerto Rico were also among those 17 states.

media.credit: Juan Vazquez, lithographer · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Vazquez, lithographer

questions.description: A painting that always shows up to parties well wrapped up.
questions.question: I'm a woman lying on a couch in a short jacket and sash. Goya painted my twin in the same pose, but with no clothes on. Which painting am I?
hints: Goya painted me in the early 19th century.
I hang in the Prado Museum, next to my twin.
My title says the exact opposite of my sister's.
questions.fun_fact: Both majas belonged to Manuel Godoy, the powerful minister of Charles IV.

media.credit: Jorge Láscar from Australia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Láscar from Australia

questions.description: A playground ring song with more drama than an afternoon soap opera.
questions.question: You hear children in a ring singing “¿Dónde vas, Alfonso XII, dónde vas, triste de ti?”. In which century did that king live?
hints: He was the son of Queen Isabella II.
His reign began after the First Republic.
He died very young, in 1885.
questions.fun_fact: The song remembers his first wife, Mercedes, who died at 18, only five months after the wedding.

media.credit: RRRW001 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: RRRW001

questions.description: A family tree with more tangled branches than a Galician forest.
questions.question: Look at the portrait: this queen, wife of Alfonso XII, was the daughter of a sister of Isabella II, the king's mother. What was she to the king?
hints: Draw the family tree in your head.
Their mothers were sisters.
It's what you are to the children of your aunts and uncles.
questions.fun_fact: Alfonso XII married her for love, even though his mother, Isabella II, did not like the match at all.

media.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

questions.description: A palace that has changed tenants more often than a student apartment.
questions.question: You're in the Royal Palace of El Pardo, where visiting foreign heads of state stay today. Who lived here from 1940 to 1975?
hints: He was a military man.
He ruled Spain for almost forty years.
After his death in 1975, the Transition began.
questions.fun_fact: It was once a royal hunting lodge, and Carlos III had it enlarged.

media.credit: Carlos Delgado · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Delgado

questions.description: Some dark swallows that come back every school year, right on time, for the literature exam.
questions.question: In class you read Bécquer's “Volverán las oscuras golondrinas” (“The dark swallows will return”). Which literary movement does it belong to?
hints: Bécquer lived in the 19th century.
His poems are about love, dreams and deep feelings.
It's the same movement as Zorrilla's “Don Juan Tenorio”.
questions.fun_fact: His “Rimas” were published in 1871, a year after his death, thanks to his friends.

media.credit: Morhaf Aljanee · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Morhaf Aljanee

questions.description: A political system with fewer surprises than a fixed match in the schoolyard.
questions.question: During the Restoration, whenever Sagasta's Liberal Party left government, its rival, Cánovas's party, always came in. Which party was it?
hints: It was one of the two parties that took turns in power.
It stood for order, the monarchy and the Church.
Its name comes from the verb “to conserve”.
questions.fun_fact: Cánovas and Sagasta swapped power so many times that the system came to be called “turnismo” (taking turns).

media.credit: Javier Perez Montes · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Javier Perez Montes

questions.description: A writer who wanted his reviews heard from the other side of town.
questions.question: I'm made of metal, I look like a small trumpet with no valves, and I used to wake soldiers in their barracks. The author of “La Regenta” wrote under my name. What am I?
hints: I’m a wind instrument.
Leopoldo Alas used my Spanish name as a pen name for his newspaper articles.
My sound is so sharp and clear that my name comes from the word for “clear”.
questions.fun_fact: “La Regenta” is set in Vetusta, a made-up city based on Oviedo, which today has a statue of its heroine in front of the cathedral.

media.credit: Simon Burchell · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Simon Burchell

questions.description: Even the most famous squire in literature didn't walk everywhere.
questions.question: In “Don Quixote”, Sancho Panza rides across La Mancha on his faithful Rucio. What animal is Rucio?
hints: The skinny horse, Rocinante, belongs to Don Quixote, not to Sancho.
It's shorter than a horse and has very long ears.
When it complains, it brays.
questions.fun_fact: “Rucio” means light brown or grayish: Sancho named his animal after the color of its coat.

media.credit: Jebulon · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jebulon

questions.description: Kickoff, chaos and a ball that always lands where it shouldn't: a typical Ibáñez match.
questions.question: Francisco Ibáñez made a comic album about the 1978 World Cup, then more about other World Cups and the Olympics. Who are its stars?
hints: Their comic strips appeared in Bruguera's magazines.
It is Ibáñez's longest-running and most famous series.
One of them is bald, wears glasses and can disguise himself as anything.
questions.fun_fact: Ibáñez kept up the habit for decades: his two agents got albums for many World Cups and Olympic Games.

media.credit: Mohamed Hozyen Ahmed · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mohamed Hozyen Ahmed

questions.description: Before speech bubbles existed, stories were told in verse, and in a hurry.
questions.question: Aleluyas, printed sheets of panels with a rhyming couplet under each one, are grandparents of the Spanish comic. In which century were they most popular in Spain?
hints: They needed a printing press, and a cheap one too.
They sold for very little at fairs and street stalls, next to other cheap prints.
It's the century when the railway arrived in Spain.
questions.fun_fact: Their name comes from the prints that were thrown to the crowds with a shout of “¡aleluya!” during Holy Week processions.

media.credit: Willi Heidelbach · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Willi Heidelbach

questions.description: A wooden puppet whose nose grows, and an artist who never took his pencil off him.
questions.question: Salvador Bartolozzi drew Pinocchio's Spanish adventures and his rival Chapete for Calleja, then went into exile after the Civil War. In which country did he die in 1950?
hints: It was one of the countries that took in the most Spanish exiles.
Spanish is spoken there.
Its capital is one of the biggest cities in the world.
questions.fun_fact: Bartolozzi made Pinocchio almost a Spanish character, with dozens of new stories that had nothing to do with the Italian original.

questions.description: A festival named after a sea creature that, luckily, doesn't sting.
questions.question: The Medusa Festival is an electronic music festival held in summer by the beach in the province of Valencia. In which town?
hints: It's south of the city of Valencia.
It sits at the mouth of the Júcar River, with a castle on top of a hill.
Its name starts with “Cu”.
questions.fun_fact: The Medusa Festival started in Cullera in 2014 and brings together DJs from all over the world.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: A singer who calls you on the phone and won't hang up, not even in summer.
questions.question: She came out of Operación Triunfo 2017 and sings “Teléfono”, “Mon amour” and “Los Ángeles”. What's her name?
hints: She's from Catalonia.
Her name is also the name of a mountain range in Alicante.
Her name starts with “Ai”.
questions.fun_fact: Aitana came second in Operación Triunfo 2017, which was won by her fellow contestant Amaia.

media.credit: Barcex · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Barcex

questions.description: A band named after a very, very old turtle, and it hasn't fallen behind one bit.
questions.question: Which of these songs is NOT by Vetusta Morla?
hints: The odd one out is also by a Spanish indie band.
The odd one out is by La Casa Azul.
It's the one about a revolution.
questions.fun_fact: Vetusta Morla takes its name from the giant turtle Morla in “The NeverEnding Story”.

media.author: Black Kite

questions.description: From dancing like a gorilla to singing like a diva: a true leap in evolution.
questions.question: Melody sang “El baile del gorila” as a child and went to Eurovision 2025 with “Esa diva”. Which province is she from?
hints: She’s from Andalusia.
She’s from Dos Hermanas, very close to her province’s capital.
Her province is home to the Giralda.
questions.fun_fact: Melody was about 10 years old when “El baile del gorila” became a hit all over Spain.

media.credit: Michael Doherty · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Doherty

questions.description: Two months staring at water, and finally someone looks up from their phone… sorry, from the horizon.
questions.question: Before dawn on October 12, 1492, after two months at sea, the lookout on the Pinta spotted something far away. What did he shout?
hints: It was exactly what every sailor had been longing to hear for weeks.
What he saw wasn't another ship or a sea monster.
For a tired sailor, it's the opposite of “sea”.
questions.fun_fact: Tradition says the lookout was called Rodrigo de Triana and never got the reward promised to the first man to sight land.

media.credit: Alelanza · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alelanza

questions.description: Philip II's great rival, who left his marriage proposal on read.
questions.question: She never married, Shakespeare's plays premiered during her reign, and her fleet fought the Spanish Armada in 1588. Which country was Elizabeth I queen of?
hints: Her country is an island… or almost.
Her father was Henry VIII, the one with six wives.
Its capital is London.
questions.fun_fact: Philip II became king consort of England by marrying Mary Tudor, Elizabeth's older half-sister.

media.credit: Cornelis Verbeeck · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cornelis Verbeeck

questions.description: The strictest customs office of the 16th century: nobody left for the Indies without stopping at the counter.
questions.question: Founded in Seville in 1503, it controlled the ships and goods sailing to and from the Americas and registered every traveler. What was it?
hints: It was a trade institution of the Catholic Monarchs.
Pilots were also trained and maps drawn there.
Its name sounds like the Spanish for signing contracts.
questions.fun_fact: In 1717 it moved to Cádiz, because ever-bigger ships struggled to sail up the Guadalquivir.

media.credit: Benjamin Smith · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Benjamin Smith

questions.description: A meeting with the boss that didn't exactly end in a promotion.
questions.question: Martin Luther, a German monk, criticized the sale of indulgences. In 1521, Charles I of Spain made him come to Worms. Why?
questions.answer: To make him take back his ideas
wrong_answers: To make him a royal adviser
To have Luther crown him emperor
To have him lead his troops
hints: Charles I defended the Church of Rome.
Luther's ideas were dividing the Christians of Germany.
The emperor wanted him to back down.
questions.fun_fact: Luther refused and, later hiding in Wartburg Castle, translated the New Testament into German.

media.credit: Hubert Berberich (HubiB) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hubert Berberich (HubiB)

questions.description: A divorce so famous it ended up starting its own church.
questions.question: I was born because an English king wanted to divorce a daughter of the Catholic Monarchs and the Pope said no. That king became my head. What am I?
hints: It all happened in the 16th century, around the same time Luther was breaking with Rome.
Today the British monarch is still my head.
My name comes from the Latin word for “English”.
questions.fun_fact: Before he broke with Rome, the Pope had given Henry VIII the title “Defender of the Faith” for writing against Luther.

media.credit: Hans Musil · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hans Musil

questions.description: A reader so hooked on novels that he ended up leaving home with a barber's basin on his head.
questions.question: Don Quixote was one, didn't pay certain taxes, and thought working with his hands was beneath him. What was a hidalgo?
hints: He belonged to the privileged class.
He had no title like duke or count.
The word comes from «hijo de algo», “son of something”.
questions.fun_fact: In “Lazarillo de Tormes”, a hidalgo so poor he had nothing to eat walked the streets with a toothpick in his mouth so people would think he had eaten well.

media.credit: Jebulon · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jebulon

questions.description: Moctezuma was expecting visitors, just not gentlemen in armor from across the sea.
questions.question: Moctezuma ruled Tenochtitlan when Hernán Cortés arrived. Which city was later built on its ruins?
hints: Today it is a country's capital.
It is one of the most populous cities in the world.
The city has the same name as the country.
questions.fun_fact: Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco and was bigger than almost every European city of its time.

media.credit: Gary Todd · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gary Todd

questions.description: The unluckiest kid in all of Spanish literature when it comes to picking a boss.
questions.question: In “Lazarillo de Tormes”, Lázaro serves several masters. Which of these was NOT one of them?
hints: It's a picaresque novel where Lázaro tells his own life story.
Later he also sells indulgences for a pardoner and carries water for a chaplain.
None of his masters ever cut his hair.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this book, “lazarillo” became an everyday Spanish word for a person or dog who guides a blind person.

media.credit: SGGREDIAGA · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SGGREDIAGA

questions.description: 1492: a year with more headlines than a whole evening news show.
questions.question: In 1492, Isabella the Catholic conquered Granada, backed Columbus and signed a decree with Ferdinand. Which group had to convert or leave Spain because of it?
hints: They had lived in Spanish cities for many centuries.
Their descendants are the Sephardim.
They prayed in synagogues.
questions.fun_fact: Many Sephardim kept speaking Judeo-Spanish for centuries, a form of the Castilian of that time.

media.credit: Superpoor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Superpoor

questions.description: A neighborhood in Cádiz where even the seagulls sing por soleá.
questions.question: I was born in 1848 in the Santa María neighborhood of Cádiz, worked at the slaughterhouse, and famous malagueñas bear my nickname. Who am I?
hints: I'm from the city of chirigotas and Carnival.
My malagueñas sound solemn, almost like a church chant.
My nickname is the Spanish word for a twin.
questions.fun_fact: The Santa María neighborhood was also the birthplace of Chano Lobato, famous for his witty, cheerful alegrías.

media.credit: Michal Osmenda from Brussels, Belgium · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michal Osmenda from Brussels, Belgium

questions.description: A festival poster that could pass for a seafood restaurant menu.
questions.question: Which of these flamenco artists does NOT have a stage name that is a sea creature?
hints: Three of them could end up in a paella.
One is shellfish with claws, one is small and pink, and one is a fish.
The one you want is a singer from San Fernando whose name starts with “Niña”.
questions.fun_fact: Camarón de la Isla got his nickname as a child because he was very blond and skinny, like a little shrimp (camarón).

media.author: Joe Mabel (on Flickr as Joe Mabel from Seattle, US)

questions.description: A trophy Spain waited for even longer than the last bus of the night.
questions.question: Rodri won the Ballon d'Or in 2024. How many years had it been since a Spanish player last won it?
hints: The previous Spanish winner was playing for Barça when he won it.
It's more than half a century.
It was Luis Suárez Miramontes, in 1960.
questions.fun_fact: Luis Suárez Miramontes, the previous Spanish winner, was from Galicia and played for Barça when he received it in 1960.

media.author: Arne Müseler, cropped by Blackcat

questions.question: In Berlin in 2024, which Spain captain lifted this trophy?

His surname starts with “mora”, the Spanish word for blackberry.
questions.fun_fact: Morata is Spain's all-time top scorer at the Euros, with 7 goals.

media.author: Кирилл Венедиктов

questions.description: The country that invented the game is still waiting for it to come home.
questions.question: Spain beat England 2–1 in a European Championship final. In what year?
hints: Spain won every one of its games at that tournament.
The final was played in Germany.
Lamine Yamal was 17 at the time.
questions.fun_fact: England lost two European Championship finals in a row: to Italy in 2021 and to Spain in 2024.

media.author: Krzysztof Popławski

questions.description: However much you grow, some nicknames never have a birthday.

hints: He was a fast, blond striker.
He later played for Liverpool and Chelsea.
They called him “El Niño” (the Kid).
questions.fun_fact: Fernando Torres also scored in the Euro 2012 final, becoming the first player to score in two Euro finals.

media.credit: Fernandopascullo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fernandopascullo

questions.description: It rains so much in Manchester that goalkeepers should get gloves with built-in umbrellas.
questions.question: How many seasons did goalkeeper David de Gea play for Manchester United?
hints: He arrived from Atlético de Madrid when he was very young.
He signed in 2011.
He left in 2023.
questions.fun_fact: Manchester United fans voted De Gea the club's player of the season four times, a club record.

media.credit: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arne Müseler

questions.description: While your friends do their middle school homework, you're stopping strikers in the Champions League.
questions.question: I'm a Barça center-back, born in 2007 in a village in Girona, and I debuted for the first team at 16. Who am I?
hints: I'm the youngest of the four.
I came up through La Masia.
My first name is Pau.
questions.fun_fact: Cubarsí comes from Estanyol, a tiny village in Girona with only a few hundred people.

media.author: Dominic Nelson

questions.description: A fiesta where artists spend months on a work that lasts exactly one night.
questions.question: In Alicante, every June, huge figures made of cardboard and wood go up in the streets and are burned on San Juan night. What is this fiesta called?
hints: It's not the Valencian fiesta in March, even though the two look alike.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: Clink that glass… but check what's inside it first.
questions.question: A widespread superstition in Spain says that making a toast with this drink brings bad luck. Which drink is it?

It's the one with no sugar, no bubbles and no flavor.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word “brindis” (toast) comes from the German “bring dir's”, meaning “I offer it to you”.

media.credit: PattayaPatrol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PattayaPatrol

questions.description: A wish list with a very short expiration date.
questions.question: On the night of San Juan, many people write their wishes, or the bad things they want to leave behind, on paper. Where does the paper go?

media.credit: Naoharu · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Naoharu

questions.description: A writer from Úbeda with more train tickets than a travel agency.
questions.question: Which of these cities does NOT appear in the title of any book by Antonio Muñoz Molina?
hints: One of his essays travels back to the time of the Umayyad caliphs.
His novel “Winter in…” mixes jazz, love and a Portuguese capital.
The missing city is the one with the Eiffel Tower.
questions.fun_fact: Muñoz Molina turned his hometown of Úbeda into “Mágina,” the imaginary city of several of his novels.

His detective is called Héctor Belascoarán Shayne.
questions.fun_fact: The Semana Negra awards the Hammett Prize for the best crime novel written in Spanish.

It grows very slowly, a little more every year.
It has a trunk, branches and leaves.

It goes “ding, dong” when it's time for Mass.

My city is famous for marzipan and for El Greco.
questions.fun_fact: The Alcázar of Toledo also houses the Library of Castilla-La Mancha, one of the largest in the region.

media.author: NorbertNagel

questions.description: A wavy ceiling so long you could miss your flight just staring at it.
questions.question: You're in Terminal 4 of Madrid-Barajas Airport, under its wavy bamboo ceiling. In what year did it open?

It was a few years before Spain won its first soccer World Cup.
It opened in the middle of the first decade of the 21st century.
questions.fun_fact: In 2006 it won the Stirling Prize, one of the most important architecture awards in the world.

questions.question: Look at this pink stone basilica surrounded by green mountains. Where is it?
hints: It's in northern Spain, near the Picos de Europa.

It's in Asturias, next to the cave of the Santina.
questions.fun_fact: The basilica was built of pink limestone and finished in 1901.

questions.question: Look at these ruins of Medina Azahara, near Córdoba. Who was this palace city built for in the 10th century?
questions.answer: For the caliph and his court
hints: At that time, Córdoba was part of al-Andalus.
It was the seat of the most powerful Muslim ruler on the Iberian Peninsula in his day.
Abd al-Rahman III ordered it built.
questions.fun_fact: Medina Azahara was looted and abandoned less than a century after it was built, and today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: Look at this building by Gaudí in Barcelona, which has been under construction for more than 140 years. What is it for?
wrong_answers: For a king to live in
hints: Thousands of people fit inside, and colored light shines in through the windows.
Its tallest tower, dedicated to Jesus, is topped by a large cross.
It's a church: the Sagrada Família.
questions.fun_fact: Gaudí is buried in the crypt of the Sagrada Família.

media.author: Didier Descouens

questions.description: A garden game for people with wigs, fans and plenty of free time.
questions.question: This detail is from “Blind Man's Buff” (“La gallina ciega”), a cartoon Goya painted as a model for a tapestry. In which royal palace was that tapestry meant to hang?
hints: It is on the outskirts of Madrid, next to a forest where the kings went hunting.
Today it hosts foreign heads of state on visits to Spain.
It shares its name with a hilly forest north of Madrid full of holm oaks and deer.
questions.fun_fact: In the painting, the blindfolded boy isn't reaching out with his hands: he's trying to touch the others with a big wooden spoon.

questions.description: Being a genius's brother-in-law has its perks… and its arguments at family dinners.
questions.question: I was born in Zaragoza in 1734, painted frescoes on domes of the Pilar and ceilings of the Royal Palace, and my sister Josefa married Goya. Who am I?
hints: I ended up as director of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando.
My younger brother, Ramón, was a painter too.
Goya worked under me at the Pilar, and we ended up arguing about the way he painted.
questions.fun_fact: Goya painted his portrait in 1795, the year Bayeu died, and today it hangs in the Prado.

media.author: David Abián

questions.description: Clothesline physics applied to the rooftops of Barcelona.

hints: I appear again and again in the attic of La Pedrera.
Because I only work in compression, I hardly need buttresses.
My name comes from the Latin word “catena”.
questions.fun_fact: Gaudí hung his models upside down, photographed them and then looked at the photos flipped over to see what the building would look like.

questions.question: Three Eduardo Chillida sculptures are fixed into the rocks where the waves break, at the end of Ondarreta beach in San Sebastián. What are they made of?

questions.fun_fact: The square next to the sculptures has holes in the ground, and when the sea is rough, air and water shoot up out of them.

Its outside is left to weather on purpose.
Its layer of rust protects it and keeps it from rusting on the inside.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Aranda, Carme Pigem and Ramon Vilalta were the first trio to win the Pritzker Prize together.

questions.question: In 1969 Salvador Dalí drew the Chupa Chups logo: red letters on a yellow flower. Which flower is it?
hints: It's a very common flower in meadows.

questions.fun_fact: Dalí suggested putting the logo on top of the lollipop so it could always be seen in full.

hints: Millares was born in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria and was fascinated by Guanche mummies.
It is a rough brown cloth made of jute.
Potato sacks are made of it.
questions.fun_fact: Millares called one series of his works “Homunculi,” figures that look as if they were made of patched rags.

Gardeners look after it, not dog groomers.

questions.fun_fact: Dressing it takes about 38,000 plants, watered by a system hidden inside the sculpture.

It was the last year of that decade.
